parole.significato: forms the diminutive of certain words; often the meaning changes unpredictably
parole.testo: Variant of -et, originally from Burgundy. See Burgundian -ôt. From Vulgar Latin *-ottum.
Inherited from Middle French abime, from Old French abisme from Vulgar Latin *abyssimus, a superlative of abyssus (“bottomless pit”), from Ancient Greek ἄβυσσος (ábussos).

parole.significato: to water (cattle, fields etc.), give water to (a person)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *abbiberāre, derived from Latin bibere (“to drink”).

Inherited from Old French abisme, from a Late Latin *abīsmus (or similar; compare Spanish, Portuguese abismo), a formally unclear alteration of Latin abyssus (“bottomless pit”), from Ancient Greek ἄβυσσος (ábussos). Doublet of abysse.

parole.significato: to calm down, to quiet down
parole.testo: From a- + Old French coisier, from Vulgar Latin *quietiare.
Inherited from Middle French accomplir, from Old French acomplir, from Vulgar Latin *(ac)complīre, from Latin complēre.
Inherited from Middle French accorder, from Old French acorder, from Vulgar Latin *accordāre, from Latin concordāre , with con- replaced by ad-. By surface analysis, accord + -er.
Inherited from Old French acoillir, from Vulgar Latin *accolligere, from Latin ad- + colligere. Cognate with Catalan acollir, Italian accogliere, Occitan aculhir, Portuguese acolher, Spanish acoger.

parole.significato: aitch, The name of the Latin script letter H/h.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French ache, from Old French ache, from Vulgar Latin *acca, probably an extension of earlier ha, from an unidentified source. Compare Italian acca.
Inherited from Old French acheter, from Vulgar Latin *accaptāre, from Latin acceptāre. Doublet of accepter.
Inherited from Middle French achever, from Old French achever, from Vulgar Latin *accapāre. Compare English achieve.
Inherited from Middle French acquerir, from Old French acquerir, aquerre, from Vulgar Latin *acquaerere, from Latin quaerere. Compare also quérir, conquérir.
Inherited from Middle French acquest, from Old French aquest, from Vulgar Latin *acquaesitum.
Relatinized from Old French amonester /amonéter, from Vulgar Latin *admonestāre, ultimately from Classical Latin admoneō.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *addonāre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *affībulāre, from Latin fībula (“clasp, brooch”).
Inherited from Old French aacier, from Vulgar Latin *adacidare, from Latin acidare, influenced by Old French agu (“needle”) (modern aigu).

Inherited from Old French ahan, from Vulgar Latin *afannō, of unknown origin. Indirectly attested by the Old French ahaner and the Old Occitan afanar. Since afannō is a verb, ahan is likely a deverbal of ahaner, although ahan is attested first.

Inherited from Old French aigre, from Vulgar Latin ācrus (possibly via a southern Gallo-Romance dialect), from Latin ācer (with a change in declension), from Proto-Italic *akris, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱrós (“sharp”). Doublet of âcre, which was borrowed from Latin.

parole.significato: to sharpen (of a point, to make sharper)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French aguisier, from Vulgar Latin *acutiāre, from Latin acūtus, the past participle of acuō. Compare Catalan agusar, Italian aguzzare, Occitan agusar, Portuguese aguçar, Spanish aguzar. The initial -ai- can probably be explained through a hypothetical proto-French or late Vulgar
From Vulgar Latin *adimantem, a form of *adimās, from Latin adamās (“hard iron”). See also diamant.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *inguinem, a masculine form of the Classical Latin neuter noun inguen.

parole.significato: any alloy based on copper; bronze
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French arain, from Vulgar Latin *arāmen, variant of Late Latin aerāmen, derived from Latin aer-. Cognate with Catalan aram, Italian rame, Occitan aram, Portuguese arame, Romanian aramă, Sardinian arràmene, Sicilian ramu, Spanish alambre (“wire”).
Inherited from Old French aisele, inherited from Vulgar Latin *axella, Late Latin ascella, from Latin axilla.
Inherited from Old French ajoster, from Vulgar Latin *adiuxtāre, *adjuxtāre, from Latin ad + iuxta. Compare also ajuster.

From Vulgar Latin *allevamen, equivalent to allevare + -men; allevare ("to raise up") took on the sense of "to raise (young)" in Vulgar Latin under the influence of elevare (“to educate”). The -i- reflects the influence of nutrimen.

parole.significato: to attract, appeal, allure, tempt; entice, draw in
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French alechier, probably from a Vulgar Latin root *allecticāre, from Latin allectāre.

parole.significato: to ream (a hole; to use a reamer or boring machine to drill or enlarge a hole or cavity)
parole.testo: From Old French alaisier (“enlarge, extend”), derived from Vulgar Latin *allātiō (“enlarge”), from Classical Latin lātus (“wide, broad”).
Inherited from Old French alesne, from Vulgar Latin *alisna (“awl”), from Frankish *alisnu, *alasnu (“awl”). Doublet of lésine.
Inherited from Old French almande, from Vulgar Latin *amend(u)la, from Latin amygdala, from Ancient Greek ἀμυγδάλη (amugdálē). Doublet of amygdale and mandorle.
Inherited from Old French amistiet, from Vulgar Latin *amīcitātem, derived from Latin amīcus (“friend”).

parole.significato: to cushion, absorb, soften (shock, blow etc.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French amortir, from Vulgar Latin *admortīre, derived from Latin mortuus (“dead”). By surface analysis, a- + mort + -ir.

Inherited from Middle French amoureux, from Old French amoreus, amereus, from Vulgar Latin *amōrōsus, derived from Latin amōrem (“love”, noun). Compare English amorous, borrowed from Middle French. Doublet of amoroso, borrowed from Italian.

parole.significato: to become mute, to disappear (of a sound)
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin *admūtīre, from mūtus (“mute, silent”). Analysable as a- + mu(et) + -ir.
Inherited from Middle French ancien, from Old French anciien, from Vulgar Latin *anteānus.
Inherited from Old French aost, from Vulgar Latin agustus, from Latin augustus. Doublet of auguste.
Inherited from Middle French appareiller, from Old French apareillier, from a Vulgar Latin *appariclāre, syncopated form of *appariculāre, probably from Latin apparāre. See also pareil.
Inherited from Middle French apprentis, from Vulgar Latin *apprenditīcius, from the past participle of Latin apprehendere.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *apprīvātiāre, from Latin prīvātus (“deprived; freed, released”), perfect passive participle of prīvō (“to bereave, deprive; to free, release”).
Inherited from Old French arbrissel, from Vulgar Latin *arbuscellum, a diminutive ultimately based on Latin arbor (“tree”).

parole.significato: archer (one who shoots an arrow from a bow or a bolt from a crossbow)
parole.testo: From Middle French and Old French archier, from Vulgar Latin *arcārius, from Classical Latin arcuārius, derived from Latin arcus (“bow”). Equivalent to arc + -er.
Inherited from Middle French ardre~ardoir, from Old French ardre~ardoir, the first from Vulgar Latin *ārdĕre and the second directly from Latin ārdēre.
Inherited from Old French ariere, from Vulgar Latin *ad retrō, from Latin ad + retrō.
Inherited from Middle French, Old French arriereban, ultimately from Vulgar Latin *ad retrō (literally “to the rear”), from Latin ad + retrō. Equivalent to arrière- (“behind”) + ban.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *arrōsāre, from Latin rōs (“dew”).

parole.significato: to stop, to come to a standstill; to halt, to stop from moving
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French arrester (“to stop”), from Old French arester (“to stay, stop”), from Vulgar Latin *arrestāre, from Latin ad- (“to”) + restō (“stop, remain behind, stay back”). Compare English arrest.

Inherited from Old French artillerie (“collection of military engins, crossbows, lances, etc.”), from artillier (“to equip, provide with contraptions”), alteration of atiller (“to arrange, adjust, put on clothes or, especially, pieces of armour”) (influenced by art), itself from a Vulgar Latin *apti
From artiller + -eur, itself from a Vulgar Latin *apticlāre, *apticulāre, from Latin aptāre (“to make capable”).

parole.significato: tree (wooden frame used in the construction of a saddle)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French, from Vulgar Latin *arciōnem (“saddlebow”), from Classical Latin arcus (“bow”). Compare Italian arcione, Portuguese arção, Spanish arzón.
Inherited from Old French assaut, asalt, from Vulgar Latin *assaltus, modification of Latin assultus.

parole.significato: to sit (someone) down, to seat, make sit
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French asseoir, from Old French asseoir, from Vulgar Latin *assedēre, re-formed from Latin assidēre, on the basis of sedeō.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *assedita, past participle of *assedere, from Latin assidēre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *assōpīre (“satisfy”), from Latin sōpiō (“to sleep”) (influenced by Old French assevir (“attain”)). Doublet of assoupir.

parole.significato: to assure, to ensure, to make sure
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French asseurer, from Old French asseürer, from Vulgar Latin *assēcūrāre, from Latin sēcūrus (“safe”). By surface analysis, a- + sûr + -er.

Inherited from Middle French astelier, hastelier, from astelle (“small piece of wood, etc., to hold a broken bone in place, splint”) + -ier (suffix denoting the location of an abode). Astelle is derived from Vulgar Latin *astella, from Latin assula (“chip; shaving; splinter (of wood)”), from assis (
Inherited from Old French ateindre, ataindre, from Vulgar Latin *attangere, alteration of Latin attingō, from tangō.

parole.significato: to harness, yoke, hitch (e.g. a horse to a wagon)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *attelare, from Latin protelare.
Inherited from Old French atisier, from Vulgar Latin *attītiāre, derived from Latin tītiō (“firebrand”).
Inherited from Old French atraire, atreire, from Vulgar Latin *attragere, from Latin attrahō.
Inherited from Old French albe, from Vulgar Latin *alba, from Latin albus (“white”).
From Old French alcun, from Vulgar Latin *alicunus, from Latin aliquī + unus. Cognate with Italian alcuno, Spanish alguno, Galician algún, Portuguese algum.
Inherited from Old French almosne, from Vulgar Latin *alēmosyna, from Late Latin eleēmosyna, from Ancient Greek ἐλεημοσύνη (eleēmosúnē, “alms”), from ἐλεέω (eleéō, “to have mercy”).

Inherited from Middle French aune, from Old French alne, from Vulgar Latin *alina, from a Germanic language, probably Frankish *alina, from Proto-Germanic *alinō. Cognate with Old High German elina, Old English eln, Old Norse alin, ǫln, Gothic 𐌰𐌻𐌴𐌹𐌽𐌰 (aleina), and Latin ulna. More at ell.

Inherited from Middle French aussi, from Old French ossi, ausi, alsi (“as, in the same way as”), from Vulgar Latin *ale si (“other so, else so”), from Latin alid, aliud (“other, another, any other, else”) + sīc (“so, thus”); probably a calque of Frankish *allswā (“as, likewise, in the same way”). From Vulgar Latin *al tantu, earlier *aliud tantum (compare with aliud), corresponding to Classical Latin alterum tantum. Compare with Old French altretant, probably evolved from this form, along with Italian altrettanto.

Inherited from Old French ostruce, according to the TLFi, from Vulgar Latin *austrūthiō, from Latin avis (“bird”) + strūthiō (“ostrich”), from Ancient Greek στρουθίων (strouthíōn). Compare Spanish avestruz and Italian struzzo.
Inherited from Old French autrui, from Vulgar Latin *alterui, alteration (after cui) of Latin alterī, dative singular of alter. Compare Italian altrui.
Inherited from Middle French advancer, from Old French avancier, from Vulgar Latin *abanteāre, from Late Latin ab ante, from Latin ab + ante.

Inherited from Middle French avec, avecques (“with”), from Old French avoc, avoec, avuec (“with”), from an assumed Vulgar Latin *aboc, *abhoc, *apud hŏque, from Latin apud (“with, near, close to”) + hoc (“this”) + -que. First used as a replacement for Latin cum (“with”) in Merovingian and Carolingia
From Vulgar Latin *adventūra, from Late Latin adventūrus, from Latin adventus.
Inherited from Old French aiol, aiuel, from Vulgar Latin *aviolus, ultimately from Latin avus.

Inherited from Middle French bac, from Old French bas, bac- (“flat boat”), of obscure origin. Possibly from Vulgar Latin *baccu (“container”), from Latin bacar (“kind of wine glass”). Or, possibly borrowed from Celtic or Germanic, from Proto-Germanic *baką (“back, rear”).

Likely named after the French town Baccarat (noted for glassmaking) in Grand Est, of ultimately unclear and debated origin. First attested in 1291 (uncertain). Inherited from Old French baignier, from Vulgar Latin *baneare, Late Latin balneāre, from Latin balneum, and probably later influenced by the related French bain. Compare Occitan banhar, Catalan banyar, Italian bagnare, Spanish bañar, Portuguese banhar.
Inherited from Old French baissier, from Vulgar Latin *bassiāre, from Late Latin bassus.
Inherited from Middle French balance, from Old French balance, from Vulgar Latin *bilancia, from Latin bilanx, from bi- (see Latin bis) and lanx.
Inherited from Old French barater (whence also English barter), possibly from a Vulgar Latin *būrattāre, of obscure origin; perhaps ultimately Celtic. Compare also Spanish and Portuguese baratar.
Inherited from Old French barbel (“barbel fish”), from Vulgar Latin *barbellus, from Late Latin barbulus, diminutive of Latin barbus (“a type of fish”).
Inherited from Old French barbu, from Vulgar Latin *barbūtus (“bearded”). By surface analysis, barbe (“beard”) + -u.

Inherited from Old French barge, from Vulgar Latin *barga, a variant of Late Latin barca, a regular syncope of Vulgar Latin *barica, from Classical Latin bāris, from Ancient Greek βᾶρις (bâris, “Egyptian boat”), from Coptic ⲃⲁⲁⲣⲉ (baare, “small boat”), from Demotic Egyptian br, from Egyptian bꜣjrb-b
Possibly from a Vulgar Latin *bardea, of Gaulish origin.
From berlong, from Old French beslong, itself inherited from Vulgar Latin *bislongus (“twice as long as it is wide”).
Inherited from Middle French bassin, from Old French bacin, from Vulgar Latin *baccinus /*baccinum, probably from Gaulish.
From Old French beve (altered based on baver), from Vulgar Latin root *baba, of imitative origin. Compare Spanish baba, Portuguese baba.
Inherited from Middle French beauté, from Old French biauté, from Vulgar Latin *bellitātem (“beauty”), from Latin bellus (“beautiful, fair”).

parole.significato: a cradle that holds a ship before and during its launch
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French berz, from Vulgar Latin *bertium (“little cradle”), from Gaulish.
Inherited from Old French bercal, from Vulgar Latin *berbicale, from *berbīx, from Latin vervex (“wether; castrated ram”).

From Old French berçuel (diminutive of bers) from Vulgar Latin berciolum diminutive of *bertium, from Gaulish *berta, from Proto-Celtic *bertā, variant of *bereti (“to carry”). Compare Old Irish bert (“bundle”). Cognate with Catalan bressol, Portuguese berço and Galician berce.

Inherited from Middle French [Term?], from Old French bercier (“to rock”), from Vulgar Latin *bertiāre, via Gaulish from Proto-Celtic *berta- (“to shake”), related to *bereti (“to carry”). See berceau (“cradle”).
Inherited from Middle French berche, from Vulgar Latin *barica, possibly a Celtic word, from Proto-Celtic *barros (“point, head, peak”).

parole.significato: large, long-handled twibill with a broad chisel and a mortise chisel for cutting mortises
parole.testo: From Old French besagües, biesagüe, from Vulgar Latin (ascia) bisacuta, from Latin bis + acūta (“double-edged”). Compare Italian bisacuto.
Inherited from Middle French besoing, from Old French besoing, from Vulgar Latin *bisonium, borrowed from Frankish *bisunnija.
From Vulgar Latin *bissus.

Inherited from Middle French biche, from Old French biche (“doe, female deer”) and bisse (“wild animal”), of uncertain origin and relation. Literally, “well come”, from Old French bienvenu, from Vulgar Latin *bene venūtus, presumably a calque of a Frankish term, from Proto-Germanic *wiljakwemô (“comer, welcome guest”), from which many modern Germanic forms, as in English welcome. Eclipsed Middle French willecomme, from Old French wileco
From Middle French biscler, from Vulgar Latin *bisoculāre, a compound of bis (“twice”) and oculus (“eye”).

parole.significato: tree trunk (chopped down, ready for sawing)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French bille, from Old French *bille (attested as Medieval Latin billia (“tree-trunk”)), from Vulgar Latin *billia, from Gaulish *bilia, from Proto-Celtic *belyom (“tree”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰolh₃yom (“leaf”). Cognate with Irish bile (“tree”), Latin folium (“leaf, foil
From Vulgar Latin bīnāre (“to do something twice; to work the land twice”), from a derivative of Latin bīnī, from bis ("twice, two times"). Cognate with Spanish binar ("to plow over").
From Old French *besel, possibly from Vulgar Latin *bisalus (“stone with two sides”), from Latin bis + ala.
Inherited from Old French blanchir, from Vulgar Latin *blancīre, a verb based on Frankish *blank.
From the Old French boscage, from Vulgar Latin *boscāticum, from Late Latin boscus, from Frankish *busk (compare Middle Dutch busch), from Proto-Germanic *buskaz (“forest, woods”).

parole.significato: calmness, tranquility (especially before a storm or something of equal intensity)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bonacia.
From Vulgar Latin *bombitire, formed from Latin bombus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bornium.

Inherited from Middle French bouchon (“bundle of hemp or foliage, oakum”), from bousche (“handful of straw, bundle of twigs”), from Vulgar Latin bosca (“brush, bundle of branches”), from Frankish *bosc (“bush”), from Proto-Germanic *buskaz (“bush”). More at bush.
From bouche + -ée, possibly Vulgar Latin *buccata, from Latin bucca. Compare Italian boccata, Romanian bucată; cf. also Portuguese and Spanish bocado.

Inherited from Middle French bouger, from Old French bougier, from Vulgar Latin *bullicāre (“to bubble; seethe; move; stir”) a frequentative based on bullīre (“to boil; seethe; roil”). Borrowed from Middle French into English as budge (“move”). Related to English boil. Compare Catalan bellugar.

Inherited from Middle French borde (“bragging, story contrived to impress”), from Vulgar Latin *burda (“contrived falsehood”), attested in a Late Latin glossary as the verb burdit (“brags, boasts”). Cognate to Provençal borda (“lie, falsehood”). Uncertain whether related to Late Latin burda (“reed,
Inherited from Old French bourjon, burjon, from Vulgar Latin *burriōnem, from Late Latin burra.
Derived from bo(u)rge (“kind of canvas”), from Vulgar Latin *burrica, from Latin burra (“shaggy garment”).

Inherited from Middle French bouton, boton, from Old French bouton, boton (“button, bud”), from Vulgar Latin *bautōnem, accusative of bautō, from Frankish *bautō (“that which pushes up, bump, knob”), from Proto-West Germanic *bautan (“to beat, push”). By surface analysis, bouter (“to push”) + -on. C

parole.significato: drover (person who drives cattle over long distances)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French buvier, from Vulgar Latin, Late Latin bovārius (“cow herder”), from Latin bovārius (“of cattle”), from bos. This form may be semi-learned, and based on bœuf, or altered from the Old French boier.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bragulare, from Latin bragere. Compare braire. Cognate with the English bray.

parole.significato: bray (to make the cry of a donkey)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bragiō, from Gaulish *bragu (compare Old Irish braigid (“to flatulate”)), from Proto-Celtic *bragyeti (“to flatulate”). Cognate with English bray.

Inherited from Middle French bransler, from Old French bransler (“to shake (a sword at), move”), a contracted form of brandeler (“to wobble”), from Vulgar Latin *brandus (“firebrand, flaming sword, sword”), ultimately from Frankish *brand (“sword”), from Proto-Germanic *brandaz (“burning, flash, fir
Inherited from Old French berbis, berbiz, from Vulgar Latin *berbicem, from Late Latin berbēcem, from Latin vervēx (“wether”).
Origin obscure. Probably borrowed through Vulgar Latin from a Germanic language, but the exact source is unclear; possibly Frankish *brāþi (“steam, vapor”).

Inherited from Old French broche, from Vulgar Latin brocca (“spike”), feminine substantive of Classical Latin broccus (“pointy-toothed or prominent-toothed”), ultimately from Gaulish, compare Old Irish brog (“awl”).
Inherited from Old French brosder, from Germanic.
From Vulgar Latin *bruncāre, *bruncus, a cross of Latin broccus (“projecting, pointed”) and truncus (“maimed, docked, truncated”).

From Middle French brosse, from Old French broce, brosse, broisse (“brushwood, brush”), of unknown origin. Probably cognate with Catalan brossa and possibly with various other Romance words. Inherited from Middle French brouiller, from Old French brouiller, from Vulgar Latin *brodiculāre, from *brodicāre (compare Lombard brodigar (“to soil, pollute”)), from Late Latin brodium (“broth, stew, mixture”), from Proto-Germanic *bruþą (“stock, broth”). More at English broth, broil.

Inherited from Old French, from Vulgar Latin *brūgere (attested in the third-person singular indicative form brugit), from a crossing of Latin rugīre (compare French rugir) + *bragere (whence French braire). Compare English burr.

parole.significato: bittern (bird of the family Ardeidae and genus Botaurus, specifically those species not formerly in the genus Ixobrychu…
parole.testo: From Middle French butor, from Old French butor, from Vulgar Latin *butitaurus, from Latin būtiō (“bittern”) + taurus (“bull”), because of its deep booming call; compare also Middle Dutch watervar (“bittern”, literally “water bull”).

Inherited from Middle French, from Old French buee (“laundry, wash”), from Vulgar Latin *būcāta (“laundry”, literally “soaked”), from Vulgar Latin *bucāre (“to soak, wash”), from Frankish *būkōn (“to soak, wash”).

parole.significato: to bang out (a task), to botch
parole.testo: Perhaps from unattested Middle French and Old French *bâcler, *bacler (“to hold in place, prop a door or window open”). From Vulgar Latin *bacculare, from Latin baculum (“rod, staff used for support”), from Proto-Indo-European *bak-. Indirectly attested in Old French desbacler (“to clear a harbour b

Inherited from Old French bast, from Vulgar Latin *bastum, derivative of *bastō (“to carry, serve as a support, suffice”), from Ancient Greek βαστάζω (bastázō, “to lift, bear”). Displaced Classical Latin clitellae.

Inherited from Middle French bastiment, from Old French bastiment (“act of building, fortification”), from bastir (“to build, make; to sew”), from Vulgar Latin *bastīre, borrowed from Frankish *bastijan (“to sew, weave”).
From Middle French bastir, from Old French bastir, from Vulgar Latin *bastīre (“to build, construct; weave, sew”), borrowed from Frankish *bastijan (“to sew, weave”).
Inherited from Old French betun, from Vulgar Latin *bittūmen, from Latin bitūmen. Doublet of bitume, a borrowing from Latin.
Inherited from Middle French busche, from Old French busche (“piece of wood to be burned”), from Vulgar Latin *busca, from Frankish *busk, from Proto-Germanic *buskaz. More at bush.
Inherited from Old French cachier, from Vulgar Latin *coacticāre, from Latin coactāre.
Inherited from Old French quailler, coaillier, from Vulgar Latin *coaglāre/ *quaglāre, from syncopation of Latin coāgulāre. Doublet of coaguler, which was borrowed.
Inherited from Old French quarel, from Vulgar Latin *quadrellus from Classical Latin quadrus. Compare Italian quadrello, Spanish cuadrillo.
Inherited from Old French quarrière, from Vulgar Latin *quadrāria, from Latin quadrāre (“to make four-corned, square; cut into a square”), from quadrus. Compare carreau. Compare also English quarry.
Inherited from Old French caresme, from Vulgar Latin *quarēsima, from Latin quadrāgēsima. Doublet of quadragésime.
From Vulgar Latin *caya (“house”)

Inherited from Middle French, from Old French cel, cil, from Vulgar Latin *ecce ille. See also celui, derived from the oblique cases of the same. The inflected forms continue Old French cest, cist, from Vulgar Latin *ecce iste.

Inherited from Old French cerise, from Vulgar Latin ceresia, from the neuter plural of Late Latin ceresium, from Latin cerasium, from Ancient Greek κεράσιον (kerásion, “cherry”), from κερασός (kerasós, “bird cherry”), ultimately possibly of Anatolian origin.
From Middle French cest, from Old French cist~cest, from Vulgar Latin *ecce iste, from Latin ecce + iste.

Inherited from Middle French chascun, from Old French chascun, from Vulgar Latin *cascunum, *casquunum, a conflation of quisque unum (“each one”) + *cata unum, a variant form showing a derivative of Ancient Greek κατά (katá) (this variant form survived into Old French as chaün). Compare Occitan cadu
Inherited from Middle French chameau, from Old French chamel, inherited from Vulgar Latin *camellus, a variant of Classical Latin camēlus (which would have yielded *chamoil).

Inherited from Old French champegnuel, from Vulgar Latin *campāniolus (“grows in the field”), from Late Latin campāneus (“relating to fields”), from Latin campānia (“level country”). The “accelerator” sense comes from the fact that accelerator pedals were initially mushroom-shaped.
From Old French cheance (“accident, chance, luck”), inherited from Vulgar Latin *cadentia (“falling”). Doublet of cadence, a borrowing from Italian.
From chapeler + -ure; chapeler derives from Vulgar Latin cappulāre, Late Latin capulāre.

parole.significato: capon; a castrated cockerel or the meat thereof
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French chappon, from Old French chapon, chiapun, from Vulgar Latin *cappōnem, from Latin cāpō. Compare Catalan capó, English capon, Italian cappone, Occitan capon, Portuguese capão, Spanish capón.

From Middle French chasque, a backformation from chascun, from Old French chascun (whence modern chacun). Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cardināria, from Classical Latin cardinem. Unrelated to French charnier.
Inherited from Old French charnu, from Vulgar Latin *carnūtus, derived from Latin carnem (“meat”). The Old French term is surface-analyzable as charn (“meat”) + -u (adjective-forming suffix).
Inherited from Old French charogne, from Vulgar Latin *carōnia, from Latin carō (“meat, flesh”). Compare Italian carogna.
Inherited from Middle French chasse, from Old French chace, deverbal of chacier.
Inherited from Old French chacier, from Vulgar Latin *captiāre, from Latin captus. Doublet of catch.
Inherited from Middle French chauffer, from Old French chauffer, chaufer, from Vulgar Latin *calfāre, from Classical Latin cal(e)facere. Compare Occitan caufar, calfar, Catalan calfar.

From Old French chauciee, chaucie, from Vulgar Latin *calciāta; there is dispute as to whether this is from Latin calx (“lime”) or its homonym, calx (“heel”) (through the verb calciāre (“stamp, tread on”)). Compare English causeway.

Inherited from Middle French chief, from Old French chief, from Vulgar Latin capus, from Latin caput (“head”), from Proto-Italic *kaput, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kauput-, *kaput-. Doublet of cap.

parole.significato: to walk on, to keep walking (especially on a long and regular or a painful walk)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cammīnāre. By surface analysis, chemin + -er.
Inherited from Old French chenil, from Vulgar Latin *canīle (“kennel”). Cognate with English kennel, Italian canile.
Inherited from Middle French chevelu, from Vulgar Latin *capillūtus. By surface analysis, cheveu (“hair”) + -u.
Inherited from Old French cheville, from Vulgar Latin *cavicla, dissimilated and syncopated form of Classical Latin clāvicula, diminutive of clāvis (“key”). Doublet of clavicule, a borrowing.
Inherited from Old French, from Vulgar Latin *capriōnem, from *capreus, cf. also caprone. Ultimately from Latin caper (“goat”).

parole.significato: to cherish, pamper, coddle (care for with affection and tenderness)
parole.testo: From Old French chuer, ultimately from Vulgar Latin cavicare.

parole.significato: bedstead (originally a large, enclosed wooden structure)
parole.testo: Old French chaelit, from Vulgar Latin *catalectus, from cata- + lectus.

Inherited from Old French chaitif, caitif, from Vulgar Latin *cactivus, from a combination of Latin captīvus (“prisoner”) with Transalpine Gaulish *caxtos, from Proto-Celtic *kaxtos (compare Irish cacht, Welsh caeth). Compare also Italian cattivo (“bad”). See also French captif, a borrowed doublet.

Inherited from Middle French chesne, from Old French chesne, chaisne, chasne, from Vulgar Latin *cassanus (attested in Medieval Latin as casnus), probably from Gaulish kassanos. Some Old French forms possibly influenced by fraisne, fresne (cf. modern frêne). Compare Occitan casse, Franco-Provençal c

From Middle French cinq, from Old French cinc, from Vulgar Latin cīnque, dissimilation of Classical Latin quīnque (“five”), from Proto-Italic *kʷenkʷe, from Proto-Indo-European *pénkʷe, cognate with Portuguese and Spanish cinco, Italian cinque. Doublet of punch.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cinctūrāre, from cinctūra (whence French ceinture). Compare the French coinage ceinturer.

Inherited from Old French cisaille(s), from a Vulgar Latin *cisac(u)la, from *caesacula, from the neuter plural of a *caesaculum, formed from the root of Latin caesus, from caedō (“cut”). Cf. also the related ciseau.

Inherited from Old French cisel, chisel, from Vulgar Latin *cisellum < *caesellum, from Latin caesus, from caedō. Compare Occitan cisèl, Catalan cisell, Italian cesello, Portuguese cinzel, Spanish cincel.

Inherited from Middle French citre, from Vulgar Latin *cithera, from Latin cithara (itself from Ancient Greek κιθάρα (kithára)), and probably influenced by sistre, from Latin sistrum. Doublet of cithare and guitare. Compare also citole.
Possibly from Vulgar Latin *cibaria, from Latin cibus.
From Old French clavel, from Vulgar Latin *clavellus (compare Italian chiavello, chiavella), from Latin clavus.

Inherited from Old French clignier, clingnier, itself probably from a Vulgar Latin *clūdiniare < *clūdināre, a derivative of clūdō, clūdere, variant of claudō (“close, shut”) (cf. French clore); it may have been phonetically influenced (transition of -ui- to -i-) in early French by descendants of cl
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cloppicāre (from cloppus), which displaced Classical claudicāre.
Inherited from Old French, from Vulgar Latin *clausiōnem, from Latin clausus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin colla, from Ancient Greek κόλλα (kólla, “glue”). Compare Italian colla, Portuguese and Spanish cola.
Inherited from Old French cumble, inherited through a Vulgar Latin form *cumlu(s) from Latin cumulus. Doublet of cumulus, a borrowing.
Inherited from Middle French commencer, from Old French comencier, from Vulgar Latin *cominitiāre.
Probably from Vulgar Latin *cōnservius, from Latin cōnservus (“fellow-slave”).
From Middle French conqueste, from Old French conqueste, cunqueste, from a Vulgar Latin *conquista, from the feminine of Latin conquisitus. Compare the masculine form conquêt.

parole.significato: to circumvent, to bypass, to skirt around
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *contornāre, from cum and tornāre. Also con- + tourner.
Inherited from Middle French contree, from Old French contree, from Vulgar Latin *(terra) contrāta (“facing land”), from Latin contrā. Doublet of country.
Inherited from Old French cunveer, cunvier, from Vulgar Latin *convitāre, from a cross between Latin invītāre (“to invite”) and convivium. Compare Italian convitare, Portuguese convidar.

Inherited from Old French convoitier, altered from the older Old French covoitier, coveitier (by analogy with the prefix con-), from Vulgar Latin *cupidietāre, a verb based on *cupidietās, a modification of the Classical Latin cupiditās by analogy with words such as medietās.
Inherited from Old French conveier (source of English convey), from Vulgar Latin *conviāre.
From a combination of Vulgar Latin *conchilia (from Latin conchylium) with coccum.
Inherited from Old French corne, from Vulgar Latin *corna (taken as a feminine singular), from Classical Latin cornua, plural of cornū (whence cor).
From Middle French cotir, from Old French cotir (“to hit; strike”), from Vulgar Latin *cottire, from Ancient Greek κόπτειν (kóptein, “to abut; bump; knock; strike repeatedly”).

Inherited from Old French coudre, cosdre, from Vulgar Latin *cōsere, from Latin cōnsuere. The original Old French infinitive was *co(u)sre, where -d- was inserted as a gliding sound. The preconsonantal -s- then became silent, in this case dropping from the spelling relatively early on. The d-spellin
From Old French coudre (“hazel”) + -ier, from coldre, epenthecized from *colre (compare foudre and soudre), from Vulgar Latin *colurus, metathesis of Latin corulus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cutina, from Latin cutis.
Inherited from Middle French couille, from Old French coille, from Vulgar Latin *cōlea n pl, from Latin cōleus m sg.
Inherited from Middle French couillu, from Old French coillu, from Vulgar Latin *cōleūtus. Compare Spanish cojudo. By surface analysis, couille + -u.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *colŏbra, altered from Classical Latin colubra, feminine counterpart to coluber (“snake”), of uncertain origin. Doublet of cobra, a borrowing from Portuguese.
Inherited from Old French colëiz, colediz, from Vulgar Latin *colātīcius, from Latin colāre. By surface analysis, couler + -is.

parole.significato: two partners in a romantic or sexual relationship
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French couple, from Vulgar Latin *cōpla, from Latin cōpula. Doublet of copule.
Inherited from Middle French corage, from Old French corage, from Vulgar Latin *corāticum, from Latin cor. Cognate with Catalan coratge, Italian coraggio, Occitan coratge, Spanish coraje.
From Vulgar Latin *curbus, from Latin curvus.
Inherited from Old French correcier, from Vulgar Latin *corruptiāre, from Latin corrumpō (whence corrompre).
From Middle French, from later Old French coissin, from Vulgar Latin coxīnus (“seat pad”), derived from Latin coxa (“hip, thigh”) with the suffix possibly after Latin pulvīnus (“pillow”).
Inherited from Old French costure, from Vulgar Latin *cōnsutūra, from Latin cōnsūtus, from cōnsuō.

Inherited from Middle French cracher, from Old French crachier (“to eject from the mouth”), from Vulgar Latin *craccare, of imitative origin, possibly via Frankish *hrākijan or *hrakkjan; compare Old High German hrahhan, hrahhjan (“to spew, spit”), Proto-Germanic *hrēkijaną (“to spit, retch, vomit”)

Deverbal of créner (“to kern”), from crenedes (“notched”), from Vulgar Latin *crinare, probably of Celtic/Gaulish origin, from Proto-Celtic *krini-, from Proto-Indo-European *krey- (“to divide, separate”). Or, less likely, from Latin cernō (“to separate”), itself from the same root.
Inherited from Middle French crier, from Old French cri(d)er, from Vulgar Latin *crītāre.
Uncertain. Perhaps from Vulgar Latin *corrutulāre, frequentative of Latin corruere. If so, cognate with Italian crollare.
First attested in Old French, corresponding to cruel + -té. Possibly from an unattested Vulgar Latin *crūdālitās, crūdālitātem (from Latin crūdēlitātem).

Origin uncertain. Derivation from the assumed Vulgar Latin *crepicella, *crepitacillum, a diminutive of crepitāculum, from crepitāre (“to crackle”) is difficult to explain from a morphological point of view. Instead, possibly from a root *krek-, *krak- (“to crack, rattle, creak, emit a bird cry”), a

parole.significato: kestrel (any of various birds of prey)
parole.testo: From Middle French cresserelle, crecerelle (“bird of prey”), usually assumed to be from crecelle (“rattle, wooden reel”) (modern crécelle), of obscure origin. Cognates possibly include: Medieval Latin clisterella f, English kestrel, Neapolitan castariello m and crestariello m, all sharing the same m
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *coquīnārium, or a later formation corresponding to cuisine + -ier.

From cable, an Old Northern French (i.e. Old Norman or Picard) variant of chable, cheable, chaable, from Vulgar Latin *caplum, contracted form of Late Latin capulum, from Latin capiō. The Norman-Picard form, used primarily in a maritime sense, coexisted with the Francien dialect forms until replacin

parole.significato: to be physically affectionate; to cuddle
parole.testo: Via Old French from Vulgar Latin *calina, which is from Latin calidus (“warm”).
Inherited from Old French damoisel, from Vulgar Latin *domnicellus, diminutive of Classical Latin dominus (“master, lord”).

Inherited from Old French dangier, alteration of Old French dongier (due to association with Latin damnum (“damage”)), from Vulgar Latin *domniārium (“authority, power”), from Latin dominus (“lord, master”).

parole.significato: in, inside (enclosed in a physical space, a group, a state)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French denz, from Vulgar Latin dē intus, from Latin dē + intus, meaning "from inside" or "from within".
From Old French dancier, from Vulgar Latin *dantiāre. Displaced the older Old French baller.
Inherited from Middle French dehors, defors, from Old French defors, from Vulgar Latin dē forīs, from Latin dē + forīs (“outdoors”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dimedius, from Latin dīmidius (“half”), derived from dis- (“apart; in two”) + medius (“middle; centre”).

Inherited from Old French damoisele, from Vulgar Latin *domnicella, diminutive of Latin domina. Compare Spanish doncella and damisela, Italian donzella and damigella, Portuguese donzela. Doublet of donzelle. See Romanian domnișoară.
From a contraction of earlier derrenier, a derivation of Old French derrain (through analogy with premier), itself derived from Vulgar Latin *dēretrānus, from Latin dē + retrō + -ānus.
From Old French devise (“division, separation; heraldic band, emblem”), from deviser. The financial sense is a semantic loan from German Devise. Compare divisa in the other Romance languages.
Inherited from Old French deviser, from Vulgar Latin *devisāre, a dissimilated form of *divisāre, from Latin dīvīsum, supine of dīvidō (“to divide”). Compare diviser.
Alteration, based on the Latin etymology, of Old French deviser, itself from a Vulgar Latin *devisāre < *divisāre, from Latin dīvīsum, supine of dīvidō (“to divide”). Compare deviser.
From Old French doleoire, from inherited from Vulgar Latin *dolatōria, from Late Latin dolatorium, from Latin dolō (“to hew”).
Inherited from Old French dunc, from Vulgar Latin dunc, from a crossing of Latin tunc with dum. Compare Italian dunque, Occitan donc and Catalan doncs.
From Old French donjon, from Vulgar Latin *dominiōnem.
Inherited from Middle French dont, from Old French dunt, from Vulgar Latin/Latin dē unde (“from where”). Compare Spanish donde (“where”).
Inherited from Middle French douzaine, from Old French dozaine, from doze (“twelve”), from Vulgar Latin *dōdeci, from Latin duodecim. Equivalent to douze + -aine.

parole.significato: to raise, to erect, to build
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French drecer, drecier, from Vulgar Latin *dīrēctiāre (through a contracted form *drēctiāre), from Latin dīrēctus (“straight”), whence the adjective direct. Compare Catalan dreçar, Italian drizzare, Sicilian addizzari, Spanish aderezar, Norman dréchi, Friulian dreçâ.
From Middle French duppe.
Deverbal from déchanter (“to descant”), from Vulgar Latin discantō, from dis- + cantō. By surface analysis, dé- + chant.
Inherited from Old French decheoir, from Vulgar Latin *dēcadere, from Latin dēcidere. Related to English decay.

parole.significato: to scorn, to despise, to disdain
parole.testo: From Old French desdeignier, from deignier (modern daigner); possibly corresponds to a Vulgar Latin *disdignāre or Latin dēdignārī. Compare to Portuguese desdenhar, Italian disdegnare and Spanish desdeñar.
Perhaps from Vulgar Latin delicāre, from Latin deliquāre, and influenced phonetically by the unrelated Old French delaier (cf. délai).

Inherited from Old French (and Middle French) deslier, from Vulgar Latin disligāre (attested in the Reichenau Glossary), from Latin dis- + ligō (“tie, bind”). Compare Occitan desligar, Catalan deslligar, Portuguese desligar, Spanish desliar, Friulian disleâ, Italian slegare, Romanian dezlega.

parole.significato: to depend (to be uncertain or contingent)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dēpendĕre, from Classical Latin dēpendēre. By surface analysis, dé- + pendre.
Inherited from Middle French destruire, from Old French destruire, from Vulgar Latin *destrugere, from Classical Latin dēstruō, from dē- (“un-, de-”) + struō (“to build”).

Inherited from Old French disner, from Vulgar Latin *disiūnāre, from disieiūnāre, disjejūnāre (“to break the fast”), from dis- + Late Latin iēiūnāre (“to fast”), from Latin ieiūnus. Doublet of déjeuner.

parole.significato: what is owed, what is due, money's worth
parole.testo: Old French deü, from Vulgar Latin *dēbūtus, past participle of Latin dēbēre. Cognate to Italian dovuto. Compare dette (“debt”), from the Classical Latin past participle dēbita n pl.
Inherited from Old French esfondrer, from Vulgar Latin *exfunderare, from fundus (“fond”). Compare Catalan esfondrar.

parole.significato: to make efforts towards, to try hard to, to endeavour
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exfortiāre, ultimately from Latin fortis (“strong”).

parole.significato: to frighten, to scare, to affray
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French effreer, from Old French esfreer, esfreder (whence also English affray), from a Vulgar Latin *exfridāre, itself of Germanic origin (with the prefix ex- added), from a Frankish *friþu (“security, peace”), from Proto-Germanic *friþuz (“peace”), from *frijōną (“to free; to

parole.significato: to place one's lips against the mouthpiece of a wind instrument
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French emboucher, from Old French embouchier. By surface analysis, en- + bouche + -er. Possibly corresponds to a Vulgar Latin *imbuccāre, from Latin bucca (compare Portuguese and Spanish embocar, Italian imboccare, Romanian îmbuca).

parole.significato: ambush (concealment in order to attack or harm someone by surprise)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French enbusque, from Old French embuschier (“to ambush”), from Vulgar Latin *imboscō, from in + boscus (“wood, woods”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *imboscāre, from in + boscus (“wood, woods”).
Inherited from Middle French emplir, from Old French emplir, from Vulgar Latin *implīre, from Latin implēre.

parole.significato: to ensnare, to entangle, to bog down
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *impastoriāre, derived from Latin pāstōrius.
From en- + chaîne + -er. Possibly also corresponds to Vulgar Latin *incatēnāre, from Latin catēnāre. Compare Italian incatenare; Catalan, Occitan, and Catalan encadenar; and Portuguese encadear.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *inclāvāre, from Latin in- + clāvis + -āre.
Inherited from Old French enclore, from Vulgar Latin *inclaudere, remodelled from Latin inclūdere. Compare the borrowed doublet inclure.
Old French desver (“to rave”), inherited from Vulgar Latin *deexvagāre, from Latin vagus.

parole.significato: to bury, to inter (something in the ground)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *infodīre, from Latin in- + fodere.
Inherited from Middle French, Old French enfraindre, from Vulgar Latin *īnfrangere, from Latin īnfringere.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ingrassiare < *incrassiare < Latin crassus. Compare Italian ingrassare, Spanish engrasar, Romanian îngrășa.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *inquaesita < Latin inquīrere. < quaerere. Compare also the Medieval Latin inquesta, from Latin in- + quaesita.

parole.significato: to teach, to instruct, to educate
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French enseignier, from Old French enseignier, from Vulgar Latin īnsignāre (also found in Medieval Latin), from Latin signāre. Compare Italian insegnare, Spanish enseñar.

From a Vulgar Latin *imptāre, contraction of *imputāre (“to graft”) (unrelated to Latin imputō (“to reckon, attribute”)), from inpotus (attested in Salic Law), from Ancient Greek ἔμφυτος (émphutos, “planted”). The Greek word may have actually reached Gaul through traders at the Mediterranean coastal

Inherited from Middle French enterrer, from Old French enterrer, from Vulgar Latin *interrāre (“to put into earth”), from Latin terra. Equivalent to en- (“into”) + terre (“earth”) + -er (infinitive marker). Cognate with English inter.

parole.significato: to wrap around, to twist around, to envelop
parole.testo: From a Vulgar Latin root *intortiliāre, from Latin tortilis (“twisted, coiled”). See also Old French entort as the past participle of entordre. Compare Catalan entortellar, Spanish entortijar, Italian intortigliare, Friulian intorteâ, cf. also Romanian întortochea.

parole.significato: to make out, see vaguely; to glimpse
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *intervidēre.
From Old French envaïr, from Vulgar Latin *invādīre, from Latin invādere.

parole.significato: to wrap someone or something, to cover
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French enveloper, from Old French envoloper, anveloper, from en- + voluper (“to wrap, wrap up”) (compare Italian -viluppare; Old Italian alternative form goluppare (“to wrap”)) from Vulgar Latin *vlopp- (“to wrap”), from Proto-Germanic *wrappaną, *wlappaną (“to wrap, roll up, t
From essaim (“swarm”) + -er. Cf. older échemer. Less likely from Vulgar Latin exāminō, exāmināre, from Latin exāmen. Compare Italian sciamare, Catalan eixamar, Spanish enjambrar, Portuguese enxamear.
Originally a dialectal (probably Picard) form of aissil, from Vulgar Latin *axīle /*axīlis, from Latin axis.

parole.significato: to dry out, to hang out to dry (e.g. washing), to spin-dry
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French essorer (whence also English soar), from Vulgar Latin *exaurare (“to rise into the air; to expose to air”), from Latin ex (“out”) + aura (“the air, a breeze”).

parole.significato: to fulfil the wish of a prayer
parole.testo: Originally a variant spelling of exhausser, from Old French exalcier, from Latin ex- + Vulgar Latin *altiāre, modelled after Classical Latin exaltāre (“raise, extol”). The sense of "fulfill (a prayer)" may have been influenced by Latin exaudīre.

Inherited from Old French esploitier (with /k/ reinserted per the Latin etymon), from earlier espleitier, from Vulgar Latin *explicitāre, a frequentative of Latin explicāre. Morphologically a doublet of expliciter.
Changed, based on the Latin root, from the original Old French estraire, from Vulgar Latin *extragere, from Latin extrahere.
From Vulgar Latin *fatidus, blend of Latin fatuus and vapidus.
Inherited from Middle French fagot.
Inherited from Middle French foible, from Old French feble, foible, from Vulgar Latin *febilis, dissimilated form of Latin flēbilis. Doublet of flébile, a borrowing. Compare English feeble.
Inherited from Middle French faillir, from Old French falir, from Vulgar Latin *fallīre, from Latin fallere. See also falloir.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fascellus, diminutive of Latin fascis (“bundle”).

parole.significato: to need, have to, to be necessary (that)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French faloir, from an earlier falleir, from a changing of Old French faillir after its third person singular, faut, earlier falt (from Latin fallit), based off the model of valoir. Faillir derives in turn from Vulgar Latin *fallīre, from Latin fallere, fallō. Compare Franco-Prove
Inherited from Old French fener, from Vulgar Latin *fenāre, from Latin fenum. Compare Occitan fenar.

Inherited from Middle French fange, from Old French fange (“mud, addle, mire”), from Vulgar Latin *fanga ~ *fangus (“mud”) of Germanic origin, see there for more. Compare Spanish and Italian fango m. Doublet of fagne (“marshland, fen”).

Inherited from Middle French faon, from Old French faon, feün, from Vulgar Latin *fētōnem, from Latin fētus (“offspring, progeny”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁(y)-. Compare Occitan fedon.
Inherited from Middle French fauchar, fauchart, from Old French fauçard, from Vulgar Latin *falcāre, derived from Latin falx (“sickle, scythe”). Doublet of faux ("scythe").

From Old French from Vulgar Latin *falcāre or *falciāre (compare Italian falciare), from Latin falcem (“sickle, scythe”) (compare faucille), from Proto-Indo-European *dhalk-, *dhalg- (“a cutting tool”).
From Old French fauchon (cognate with Italian falcione), from Vulgar Latin *falciōnem, from Latin falx.

Inherited from Old French faute, from Vulgar Latin *fallita, feminine of *fallitus, in place of Latin falsus, perfect passive participle of fallō. Compare Catalan, Spanish, and Portuguese falta. Doublet of faillite. Compare English fault and Spanish falta (“lack, shortage”).
From Old French fener + -aison, or less likely from Vulgar Latin *fenātiōnem. Compare Occitan fenason.
Derivative of the verb fendre with the suffix -iller, or less likely from a Vulgar Latin *findiclāre < *findiculāre, from Latin findō. Compare also Old Occitan fendilhar.
Inherited from Old French fenoil, from Vulgar Latin *fenuclum, syncopated form of Late Latin fēnuculum, a diminutive of Latin fēnum.

Inherited from Old French fermail (also fermeil, fermal), from Vulgar Latin *firmāc(u)lum, a noun derived from Latin firmāre (“make fast”). By surface analysis, fermer + -ail. Compare Occitan fermalh, Italian fermaglio.

Inherited from Middle French fesse f, from Old French fesse f, from Vulgar Latin *fissa f (“split, cleft”), from Latin fissum n, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰidtós. Originally referred to the gluteal cleft. The verb fesser and its derivatives are etymologically unrelated and converged towa
From Old French festeer/festeier/festoyer, inherited from Vulgar Latin *festizāre.
Inherited from Old French feüz, fadude (“one who has accomplished his destiny”), from Vulgar Latin *fatutus, from Latin fatum (“destiny”).
Inherited from Middle French feuiller + -eret, from Old French [Term?], from Vulgar Latin *fodiclāre from Latin *fodiculāre, from fodicāre, from fodere.
Inherited from Middle French feuille + -ure, from Old French [Term?], from Vulgar Latin *fodiclāre from Latin *fodiculāre, from Latin fodicāre, from fodere.
Probably from Vulgar Latin filicella, from Latin fīlum ("thread").

parole.significato: to plug in (to drive something in by its point, as with a nail or a stake)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French ficher, from Old French fichier, from Vulgar Latin *fīg(i)cāre, frequentative based on Latin fīgere (“fasten, fix”). The "give a damn" sense is a minced oath of foutre (“to fuck”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *felem m or f, from Latin fel n.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *femita < femus, altered variant of fimus (“dung, manure”). Doublet of fumier.
Inherited from Old French fier, from Vulgar Latin *fīdāre, from Latin fīdere.
Inherited from Old French fegier, from Vulgar Latin *feticāre, ultimately from Latin ficatum.
From Old French flajol (“flute”) + diminutive -et; probably from Vulgar Latin *flabeolum (“flute”), from Latin flāre (“to blow”).
Inherited from Old French flairier, from Vulgar Latin, Late Latin flāgrāre, by dissimilation from Latin frāgrāre, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰreh₂gro-, from *bʰreh₂g- (“to smell”) + *-ro-.
From Old French flambeier, inherited from Vulgar Latin *flammizāre (but influenced by flambe), derived from Latin flamma. Derivable from flambe + -oyer.

Perhaps a variant of flairer, or more likely from fleur (“odour”) (obsolete in standard modern French but still found in local dialects), from Old French flaour, flaör (whence English flavour), from Vulgar Latin *flātārī (“odour, that which blows”), from Latin flātus.
Inherited from Middle French fleche, from Old French fleche, from Vulgar Latin *fleccia, borrowed from Frankish *fliukkijā, from Proto-West Germanic *fleuk(k)ōn + *-jā.

From Middle French fleche, partly from Old French fliche, from Old Norse flikki; and partly from Picard Old French flec, from Middle Dutch vlecke, vlicke, from Old Dutch *flikki, from Proto-West Germanic *flikkī; both from Proto-Germanic *flikkiją (“piece of meat; side of bacon”). Cognate with Middl
Inherited from Old French flechir, from an original flechier (with a change in verb class), from Vulgar Latin *flecticāre, frequentative based on Latin flectere.
Inherited from Old French foire from a Vulgar Latin *fēria from the classical Latin noun fēriae.

Inherited from Old French forain, from Vulgar Latin *forānus (“outsider”), from Latin forīs (“outside”). Assimilated to foire (“fair”) (which is from Latin fēria) through folk etymology. Once meant "foreign", but replaced by étranger in this sense.
Inherited from Old French forcier, from Vulgar Latin *fortiāre, a verb based on Late Latin fortia, a noun based on Latin fortis (“strong”).
Inherited from Old French fulgiere, from Vulgar Latin *filicāria (“thicket of ferns”), from Latin filix (“fern”). Compare Catalan falguera, Occitan falguièra, Galician folgueira.
From Old French, from Vulgar Latin *fodiclāre < *fodiculāre, from Latin fodicāre, from fodere. Compare fouir.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fāgīna (“beech marten”).
From Vulgar Latin *fodīre, from Latin fodere.

parole.significato: to stamp, to impress, to dent; to mill
parole.testo: From Middle French fouller (“to trample, mill, fordo, mistreat”), from Old French foler (“to crush, act wickedly”), from Vulgar Latin *fullāre (“to trample, to full”), from Latin fullō (“fuller”). More at full.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *furicōnem, from *furicāre, from Latin furō (“to steal”).
Inherited from Old French furmi, from a Vulgar Latin *formīcus, from Latin formīca (cf. also the feminine Old French formie).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *focārium, nominalization of the Late Latin adjective focārius, from Latin focus (“hearth”).
Inherited from Middle French frais, from Old French freis, from Vulgar Latin *friscum. Related to English fresh. Doublet of fresque.
Inherited from Old French frenge, from Vulgar Latin *frimbia, metathesis of Late Latin fimbria, from Latin fimbriae.

parole.significato: to slowly mix yeast, flour and water
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French fraser, fraiser, from Old French fraser, from Vulgar Latin *frēsāre, from the Late Latin term (faba) frēsa (“ground bean”), from frēsus (“crushed”), from the verb frendō (“to crush, gnash”).
Inherited from Middle French froissure, from Vulgar Latin *frixūra, from Latin frixus (“roasted, fried”).
From a variant of Old French fru, from Vulgar Latin *frocum, from Frankish *hrōk. Compare English rook.
Probably from Vulgar Latin *frīgicāre, frequentative of Latin frīgō (“to roast, fry”), or perhaps a blend of frire (“to fry”) + casser (“to break”).
Inherited from Old French frepe, possibly from Vulgar Latin falappa. See friperie.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *frustiāre (“disperse into pieces”), from Latin frustum (“piece, fragment”).
Inherited from Middle French fremir, from Old French fremir, from Vulgar Latin *fremiō, from Latin fremō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰrem-.
Inherited from Middle French fuyr, fuir (“to flee”), from Old French fuir, from Vulgar Latin *fūgīre, from Latin fugere, from Proto-Italic *fugiō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewg-.
Remodeled, on the model of suite, from Old French fuie, from Vulgar Latin *fūgita, feminine past participle of *fūgīre, from Latin fugere. Doublet of fuie.
Inherited from Old French femier, from Vulgar Latin *femārium, from *femus, alteration of Latin fimus. Spelling influenced by fumer.

From Old French furet, furret, from Vulgar Latin *fūrittus (literally “little thief”) (compare Italian furetto), diminutive of Latin fūr (“thief”). See also Old French fuiron (“weasel, ferret”), from Vulgar Latin *fūriō, fūriōnem, from Late Latin fūrō (“cat; robber”) (compare Portuguese furão), dimi
From Old French fuisil, foisil, from Vulgar Latin *focīlis (petra), from Latin focus. Compare Italian fucile.
Inherited from Middle French fascher, from Old French faschier. Probably from Vulgar Latin *fasticāre, from an alteration of Late Latin fastidiāre < Classical Latin fastīdīre.
Inherited from Old French fae, from Vulgar Latin Fāta (“goddess of fate”), from the plural of Latin fātum (“fate”). Compare Catalan, Occitan, and Portuguese fada, Italian fata, Spanish hada.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *fagellare, from Latin flagellare. Doublet of flageller.
Inherited from Middle French gaigner, from Old French gaigner, gaaignier, itself inherited from Vulgar Latin *wadaniāre, ultimately from Frankish *waiþanōn.

parole.significato: a worker who kneads dough in a bakery
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French joindre, gaindre (direct case), inherited from Vulgar Latin *jŭnior, from Latin jūnior (nominative). Compare Old French gignor (from the Latin accusative). Doublet of junior, a recent borrowing.

Inherited from Middle French glace, from Old French glace (“ice", also "glass, mirror, radiance”), from Vulgar Latin *glacium/a, from Latin glaciēs (“ice”). The senses of "glass, mirror, radiance" were possibly derived from Frankish *glas (“glass”).
Inherited from Old French glaire, from Vulgar Latin *clāria, from Latin clarus (“clear”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *classum, from Latin classicum (“trumpet signal”).
Inherited from Old French glecte, from Vulgar Latin *glet < Latin glittus, a variant of glutus.

parole.significato: to cluck (make the noise of a chicken)
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *clociare, from Latin glocire.
It appears to be a regional derivation from Old French goitron, from Vulgar Latin *gutturiō, *gutturiōnem, from Latin guttur, or a regressive derivation from goitreux.

parole.significato: gullet, back of the throat, pharynx (the part of the throat leading to the esophagus)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French geuse, josier, from Vulgar Latin *gusia or *gausia (compare Italian gozzo (“gizzard”), Friulan gose, Romanian guşă (“maw, gullet”)), from Late Latin geusiae, from Gaulish geusiae (compare Welsh gewai (“glutton”)).
Inherited from Old French gofre, with metathesis from Vulgar Latin or Late Latin colfus, culfus, variants of colpus, from Ancient Greek κόλπος (kólpos).

Inherited from Middle French goupil, from Old French gupil, golpil, gulpil, vorpil, volpil, from Vulgar Latin *vulpīculus, alteration of Latin vulpēcula (“fox kit”), diminutive of vulpēs. Compare goupille. See also Old Italian volpiglio, Occitan volpìlh, Catalan volpell, Portuguese golpelha, Spanish
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *grāna, neuter plural of grānum reanalysed as a feminine. Compare grain.
Inherited from Old French craisse, from Vulgar Latin *crassia, from Latin crassus. Compare Occitan graissa, Catalan greix.
Inherited from Middle French grange, from Old French grange, from Vulgar Latin *grānica, from Latin grānum (“grain”).
Inherited from Middle French (g)renouille, from Old French (g)renoille, from Vulgar Latin *rānucula, diminutive from Latin rāna (“frog”).

From a crossing of gresillon and Middle French or Old French grillet (with numerous variations in French dialects; see grelet, see also grelot), probably a derivative of an early root grill- (compare Occitan grilh, Catalan grill), from Vulgar Latin *grīll(i)us, from Latin gryllus, probably from Anci

From a Vulgar Latin *grolla, of uncertain origin; the word has more common in Occitan (compare grola), Franco-Provençal, and the west of the country, from which it entered Parisian argot in the 19th century).
Inherited from Old French grumiel, from Vulgar Latin *grimellus or *grumellus, variant of Latin grumulus, diminutive of grumus, from Proto-Indo-European *gar-, *ger- (“to tie, bind together”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *grava (attested in Mediaeval Latin), of pre-Latin origin, possibly Gaulish *grawa, from Proto-Celtic *grāwā.
From Old French guerroiier, inherited from Vulgar Latin *werrizāre. Derivable from guerre (“war”) + -oyer (verb-forming suffix).
Inherited from Old French gaiant, jaiant, jaianz, from Vulgar Latin *gagantem, through assimilation from Latin gigantem, from Ancient Greek γίγας (gígas, “giant”).
Inherited from Old French genice, from Vulgar Latin *jēnicia, alteration of *iūnicia, from Latin iūnix (“young cow, calf, heifer”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *iacina, from iaceō, iacēre (whence gésir).

Inherited from Middle French hache, from Old French hache, borrowed from Frankish *happjā (“axe, hatchet”). In spite of the similar pronunciation, unrelated to Italian ascia, from Latin ascia (“axe”).
Inherited from Old French haucier, from Vulgar Latin *altiāre, derived from Latin altus (“high”).

parole.significato: to shame; to disgrace; to dishonor
parole.testo: From Middle French honnir, from Old French honir, from Vulgar Latin *haunīre (“shame, dishonor”), from Frankish *haunijan (“humble, humiliate”) (whence also honte), from Proto-Germanic *haunijaną (“to make low, humble”), from Proto-Indo-European *kaw- (“to be evil, make evil”). Cognate with Old High

Inherited from Middle French houce, from Old French hulce, from Vulgar Latin *hultia, from Frankish *hulfti, probably related to the verb *hulljan (“to cover”). Cognate with Old High German hulft (“blanket, saddlecloth”), Middle Low German hulfte, holfte (“sheath for a weapon, saddle holster, quiver
From Latin upupa, via the syncopated Vulgar Latin ūppa.

Inherited from Old French hurler, from Vulgar Latin ūrulāre, from Latin ululāre, from a reduplicated Proto-Indo-European imitative root. Doublet of hululer. The h- might be due to influence by Frankish *hūilōn, from Proto-Germanic *hūwilōną; compare English howl.
From Vulgar Latin *ericiare, from erīcius.

Inherited from Vulgar Latin illī, which sounded il in Old French, to which a plural -s was added. While il was the nominative form from late Latin, els, eus was the oblique form ("them") that had evolved from late Latin illōs, and is the ancestor of modern French eux. In Old French, "they", being a
From Middle French inciser, from Old French enciser, from Vulgar Latin *incīsāre, frequentative of incidō, incidēre

Learned modification of the inherited Old French enemisté, enemistié (whence also English enmity), itself from a Vulgar Latin *inīmicitātem, based on Latin inīmicitia, and modeled on the French amitié.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ebrionia, from ēbrius (whence ivre).
Uncertain. Possibly from a Vulgar Latin *galīre, from Transalpine Gaulish *gali- (“boil, gush, well up”).

Inherited from Old French jante, from Vulgar Latin *gambita, *cambita, borrowed from Gaulish *cambitā, from Proto-Celtic *kambitā, a derivate of *kambos (“curved”). Perhaps related to Late Latin gamba.

From Vulgar Latin *garra, from Gaulish *garra (“leg”) (compare Welsh gar), from Proto-Celtic *garros, which is of uncertain origin; possibly sharing a Pre-Greek / substrate origin with Ancient Greek ἄκαρα (ákara, “leg, shank”).
Inherited from Old French get, giet, from a Vulgar Latin *iectus, jectus, an alteration of Latin iactus (“a throwing, throw”).
Inherited from Middle French jeune, from Old French juene, juefne, from Vulgar Latin *iŏvenem, from Latin iuvenem.
From jeune + -esse; found in Old French as juenesce. Less likely from a Vulgar Latin *juvenitia. Compare Italian giovinezza.
Inherited from Old French joie, from Vulgar Latin or Late Latin *gaudia, from Classical Latin gaudium.
From Old French joe, from Vulgar Latin *ga(v)ota.
Inherited from Middle French jouir, jouïr, iouyr, from Old French joïr, from Vulgar Latin *gaudīre (*gaudiō), from Latin gaudēre. Doublet of gaudir, which was a borrowing.
From Old French jornee, from Vulgar Latin *diurnāta.
Inherited from Old French joster, from Vulgar Latin *iuxtāre, from Latin iuxtā (“close to”). See also jouxter.

parole.significato: a male adolescent, a young man
parole.testo: From earlier jouvencel, Old French jovenenciel, from Vulgar Latin *iuvencellus, from Latin iuvenculus.

parole.significato: a female adolescent, a young woman; female equivalent of jouvenceau
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *iuvencella, from Latin iuvencula.

From Middle French laid (“hideous, ugly”), from Old French laid, leid (“unpleasant, horrible, odious”), from Vulgar Latin *laitus (“unpleasant, ugly”), from Frankish *laiþ (“unpleasant, obstinate, odious”), from Proto-Germanic *laiþaz (“sorrowful, unpleasant”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyt- (“unpl
Inherited from Middle French language, from Old French language, from Vulgar Latin *linguāticum, from Latin lingua (“tongue, speech, language”) (whence langue). By surface analysis, langue + -age.
From Old French larmoiier, from Vulgar Latin *lacrimizāre. Synchronically larme (“teardrop”) + -oyer (verb-forming suffix).
Inherited from Old French lorier, from Vulgar Latin *laurārius, suffixed from Latin laurus (whence Old French lor).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *lenditem, alteration of Late Latin lendinem, itself an alteration of Classical Latin lendem.
Inherited from Old French lentille, from Vulgar Latin *lenticla, from syncopation of Latin lenticula. The "lens" meaning is because early lenses resembled lentils.
Inherited from Old French levain, from Vulgar Latin *levāmen, from levō.

parole.significato: brach, bitch hound (specifically, dog used for breeding hunting dogs)
parole.testo: Probably from Vulgar Latin *licia, from Latin lycisca, feminine of lyciscus (“wolf dog”).
Inherited from Old French [Term?] (cf. the form limaz), from Vulgar Latin *limacea, ultimately from Latin limax (“slug, snail”).
Inherited from Old French luvesche, livesche, from Vulgar Latin *levistica, from Latin levisticum, from ligusticus.

parole.significato: cork (dead protective tissue between the bark and cambium in woody plants, with suberin deposits making it impervious t…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French, from Vulgar Latin *levius, from Latin levis (“light (in weight)”).
Inherited from Old French loingtien, from Vulgar Latin *longitānus, from Latin longē. Compare Italian lontano.

Inherited from Old French loir, leir, lère, from Vulgar Latin *glirem, from Classical Latin glīrem. Compare Spanish lirón. Cf. also similar loss of initial Latin 'g-' in Old French luissel (from *globuscellum), lemoissel (from *glomiscellum).
Inherited from Middle French lors, from Old French lors, lores, from earlier lur, lor, from Vulgar Latin illā hōrā, from Latin ille + hōrā.
Inherited from Old French luëte, formed by agglutination of the article to uëte, from Vulgar Latin *ūvetta, from Latin ūva.
Inherited from Middle French luour, lueur, from Old French lueur, luur, from Vulgar Latin *lūcōrem, from Latin lūceō. Compare Italian lucore, Romanian lucoare, Catalan llugor, Occitan lugor.

parole.significato: to release; to loosen; to let go
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French lascher, from Old French laschier, from Vulgar Latin *lassicāre < *laxicāre, frequentative of Latin laxāre (whence French laisser).

Inherited from Middle French lévre, from Old French levre, earlier lavras (plural) (ca. 980), from Vulgar Latin labra, originally a neuter plural of Latin labrum, from Proto-Indo-European *leb- (“to hang down, droop”). An Old and Middle French variant, leffre, may have blended with Old High German l

Inherited from Old French legier, from Vulgar Latin *leviārius, from *levius + -ārius, the former element representing an alteration of Latin levis (“lightweight”). Compare Catalan lleuger, Occitan leugièr.
Inherited from Old French maille, from Vulgar Latin *macla, inherited from Latin macula. Doublet of macule, which was borrowed. Compare Italian maglia.

Inherited from Old French maintenir, from Vulgar Latin, Late Latin manūtenēre (“to support”), from Latin manū (“with the hand”) + teneō (“to hold”). Equivalent to main + tenir. Compare Spanish mantener, Portuguese manter, Italian mantenere.
Alteration of malastru, from Vulgar Latin male astrucus.
From Old French manier, Inherited from Vulgar Latin *manizāre. Compare Italian maneggiare, whence French manège.
From Vulgar Latin *manuoperō, from Classical Latin manus (“hand”) with operor (“to work”).
Inherited from Middle French marchand, from Old French marcheant, earlier marchedant, from Vulgar Latin *mercatantem, from the verb *mercatare, from Latin mercatus (“market”).
From Vulgar Latin *margella, from Latin margō.

Inherited from Middle French massacrer, from Old French macecrer, macecler, probably from Vulgar Latin *matteuculāre, from *matteuca (whence French massue), from *mattea or Late Latin mattia, from Latin mateola (“hoe”).
Inherited from Old French mace, from Vulgar Latin *mattia, *mattea (compare Occitan massa, Catalan maça, Italian mazza, Spanish maza, Portuguese maça), probably derived from Latin mateola (“hoe”).
Inherited from Old French massiz (with the suffix replaced by -if), from Vulgar Latin *massīcius, from Latin massa.

Inherited from Old French massüe, maçüe, earlier maçug(u)e, from Vulgar Latin *matteūca, extended from Vulgar Latin *mattia, *mattea whence masse, vulgarized from Latin mateola. Compare Romanian măciucă and Occitan maçuga.
From Vulgar Latin *mansūra, from Late Latin mānsūra.
Inherited from Old French menacier, manecier, from Vulgar Latin *mināciāre, from Latin minācia (“threat”). Equivalent to menace + -er.
Inherited from Old French *meienel, from Vulgar Latin *medianellus, from Latin mediānus (“middle, central”). Cognate with Catalan mainell.

Inherited from Middle French mensonge, from Old French mençonge, mençunge, probably from a Vulgar Latin *mentionica, from Late Latin mentiōnem (in the sense of "lie" rather than "mention"), probably formed from haplology of a root *mentītiō, from Latin mentītus, past participle of mentior. Cognate t
Inherited from Middle French menteur, from Old French menteor, menteür, menterre. By surface analysis, mentir + -eur. May correlate to a Vulgar Latin *mentitōr, mentitōrem, from Latin mentior.

Inherited from Old French menton, mentun, from Vulgar Latin *mentō (accusative *mentōnem), from Classical Latin mentum. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to project”). Compare Occitan menton, Catalan mentó, Romansh mintun.

parole.significato: to do craftwork or small handiwork
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French menusier, from Vulgar Latin *minūtiāre, from Latin minūtus (whence French menu).

parole.significato: oak stave (used to make barrels, etc.)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin materiāmen, from materia + -men.
Inherited from Old French miche, from Vulgar Latin *mīcca, from Latin mīca (“crumb”) via expressive gemination of /k/. Doublet of mie and mica.
Inherited from Middle French miel, from Old French miel, Vulgar Latin *melem m or f, from Latin mel n.

Inherited from Old French mincier, of disputed origin. Often purported to be from Vulgar Latin *minūtiāre, a verb based on Latin minūtus, though the phonetic development poses several problems. The proper outcome of Vulgar Latin *minūtiāre is rather the Old French menusier, menuiser (“to reduce to s
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *mina, Gaulish *meina (see also Welsh mwyn, Middle Irish míanach (“ore”)), from Proto-Celtic *meinis (“ore, metal”).

From an alteration of Old French moilon (influenced by moelle), itself probably from a Vulgar Latin *mūtuliōnem, from Latin mūtulus (“stone or wood overhang”). Compare Italian modiglione; cf. also Spanish mojón. Doublet of modillon, taken from Italian.
Inherited from Old French moiste, muste, from a cross between Vulgar Latin *mucidus (from Latin mūcidus) with forms of mustum; cf. *mustidus.

parole.significato: my (used to qualify masculine nouns and vowel-initial words regardless of gender)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French mon, from Old French mun, mon, meon, from Vulgar Latin, Late Latin mum, a reduced variant of Latin meum, accusative masculine and neuter singular of meus. Probably influenced by Gaulish mon (“my”).

parole.significato: to go up, to climb (go to a higher position)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French monter, from Old French monter, from Vulgar Latin *montāre, from Latin montem (“mountain”).
Inherited from Old French mordre, from Vulgar Latin *mordĕre, from Latin mordēre.
Inherited from Middle French, from Old French mort, from Vulgar Latin *mortu, from Latin mortuus.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *muccāre, from mucus.

parole.significato: to make wet, get wet, dampen, moisten
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French moillier, from Vulgar Latin *molliāre (“soak”), a verb based on Latin mollis (“soft”). Compare Occitan molhar.
Inherited from Old French moule, from Vulgar Latin *mŭsclus, from Latin mūsculus. Doublet of muscle.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *murāginem, related to Spanish murajes, Portuguese morugem, Galician muruxa.
Inherited from Middle French mouton, from Old French mouton, from Vulgar Latin moltō, from Gaulish *multon-, from Proto-Celtic *moltos.
Inherited from Middle French masle, from Old French masle, from Vulgar Latin masclus, contracted form of Latin masculus.
Inherited from Old French mastin, inherited from Vulgar Latin *māns(u)etīnus (“tamed (animal)”), from Classical Latin mānsuētus (“tamed”). Cognate to English mastiff.

Probably from regional mégauder (“to suckle”), from mégaud, from mègue (“whey”), from Vulgar Latin *mesga, from Gaulish (compare Old Irish medc (“whey”), Welsh maidd (“whey”), Cornish meith (“whey”)), from Proto-Celtic *mezgos (“whey”), from Proto-Indo-European *mesgos (“marrow”).
Vulgar Latin *mistilium.

Inherited from Old French mestier, inherited from Vulgar Latin *misterium, a syncopated form of ministerium (whence French ministère). Compare Portuguese mister, also mester, Italian mestiere, Spanish and Catalan menester.

Inherited from Middle French mesme, from Old French mesme, earlier medesme or medisme and meïsme, from Vulgar Latin *metipsimus, from Latin -met + ipse + -issimus. Cognates include Bourguignon moîme, Spanish mismo, Portuguese mesmo and Italian medesimo.
From an alteration of Old French meure, from Vulgar Latin *mōra, from Latin mōrum, from Ancient Greek μόρον (móron).
Probably from Vulgar Latin *nārificō, a humorous derivation of Latin nāris (“nose”). through an intermediate Occitan nariguar.
Inherited from Old French narille, from Vulgar Latin *nārīcula, diminutive of Latin nāris.
Inherited from Old French narine, from Vulgar Latin *narina, from Latin nāris.
Inherited from Middle French nate, from Old French nate, from Vulgar Latin *natta, variant of Latin matta, from Punic or Phoenician (compare Hebrew מיטה \ מִטָּה (mitá, “bed, couch”)).

Inherited from Middle French navire, from Old French navirie, variant of navilie, probably from Vulgar Latin *navilium (compare Old Occitan navili), alteration of Classical Latin navigium (whence also Old French navoi, navie). Cognates with Catalan nau, Galician nave, Italian nave, Occitan nau, Port
Inherited from Middle French neiger, from Old French negier, from Vulgar Latin *nivicāre, a verb based on Latin nivem (“snow”, noun). Compare Italian nevicare.
From earlier noirprun, from Vulgar Latin *niger prūnus.

Inherited from Middle French nettoyer, from Old French netoiier, a restructuring (based on net (“clean (adj.)”)) of Old French noiier (“to clean”), from Vulgar Latin *nitidiāre, a verb based on Latin nitidus (“shining, polished”), which took on the meaning of 'clean'. By surface analysis, net + -oye
Inherited from Old French niés, from a Vulgar Latin *nīdācem, derived from nīdus (“nest”) + -āx.
Inherited from Old French nigier, from Vulgar Latin nīdicāre (Classical Latin nīdificāre), from nīdus (“nest”).
Inherited from Old French nivel, livel, from Vulgar Latin *libellus m, from Latin lībella f. Cognate with English level, Spanish nivel, and Portuguese nível.
Inherited from Old French noce, noces, from Vulgar Latin *noptiās, from Latin nuptiās.
Inherited from Old French, from Vulgar Latin *nigricīre, from Latin nigrēscere.

Inherited from Middle French nombril, from Old French nonbril, from Vulgar Latin *umbilīculus (compare Occitan embonilh), from Latin umbilīcus. The initial n is probably due to an interference from possessive determiners: Old French mun onbril (“my navel”) → mun nonbril (i.e. a rebracketing). Compar

Inherited from Middle French nouvelle, from Old French novele, from Vulgar Latin *novella, substantivized neuter plural form of Latin novellus (“new, novel”). Compare Italian novella. Doublet of novelle.
From Vulgar Latin nucārius (“nut tree”) from Classical Latin nux. Compare Spanish noguera, Portuguese nogueira, Catalan noguera, Occitan noguièr. Equivalent to noix + -ier.

parole.significato: huzzah, hurrah (cry of celebration in portrayals of medieval people)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French Noël, from Old French Noel, Naël, inherited from Vulgar Latin *notālis, from Latin nātālis [diēs Dominī] (“birthday of the Lord”) with dissimilation of the first -a- to -o-. Doublet of natal.
Inherited from Middle French nue, from Old French nue, from Vulgar Latin *nūba, from Latin nūbēs. Compare Occitan niu; Portuguese nuvem; Spanish and Italian nube.
Inherited from Old French nuire, from Vulgar Latin *nocĕre, from Latin nocēre (whence Old French nuisir).
From the Old French adverb nuitantre, nuitant (plus the suffix -amment), from Vulgar Latin, Late Latin noctanter, from Latin nox.
From Vulgar Latin *nespirum, from Latin mespilum, from Ancient Greek.

Inherited from Middle French occire, from Old French ocire (with /k/ reinserted per the Latin etymon), from Vulgar Latin *auccīdō, altered from Latin occīdō, possibly by influence of another verb such as auferō.
Inherited from Old French ofrir, from Vulgar Latin *offerīre, from Latin offerre.

From Vulgar Latin augīvus, from Latin augēre, as the ogive goes on increasing, and the arch it forms increases the strength of the vault. In Old French we find the phrase arc ogif, itself from Latin arcus augivus. The word was also written as augive in the 17th century.

Inherited from Old French oie, from earlier oe, oue, from Vulgar Latin auca, contraction of *avica, from Latin avis (“bird”). Compare Italian, Spanish, and Catalan oca, Franco-Provençal ôye, Occitan and Romansh auca, Friulian ocje. The Trésor de la langue française argues that -i- was added by the e
Inherited from Middle French oncle, from Old French oncle, from Vulgar Latin *aunclum, from Latin avunculus.
From Old French ondoiier, inherited from Vulgar Latin *undizāre. Derivable from onde + -oyer.
Inherited from Old French, from Vulgar Latin *ungla, syncopated form of Latin ungula, from unguis, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃negʰ-.
From Middle French ore, from Old French ore, from Vulgar Latin hā horā, alteration of hāc horā (“(in) this hour”, ablative). Compare Italian ora, Spanish ahora, Portuguese agora.
Inherited from Old French orage m, from Vulgar Latin *aurāticum m, derived from Latin aura f (“wind, breeze”).

Inherited from Middle French oreille, from Old French oreille, from Vulgar Latin oricla, from Latin auricula, diminutive of auris, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ṓws. Cognate with Catalan and Galician orella; Portuguese orelha; Italian orecchio; Occitan aurelha; Romanian ureche; and Spanish
From Vulgar Latin hā horā, from Latin hac hora.
From Vulgar Latin *hordeata (“drink made of barley”); by surface analysis, orge (“barley”) + -ade

Inherited from Middle French orgueil, from Old French orgoil, from Vulgar Latin *orgollium, borrowed from Proto-West Germanic *uʀgōllju, from Proto-Germanic *uzgōljō. Cognate with Old High German urguol (“outstanding, distinguished”), Old Saxon urgôl (“outstanding, distinguished”), Old English orgel
Inherited from Old French orle, from Vulgar Latin *ōrula, a diminutive of Latin ōra (“edge”), probably from ōs, ōris (“mouth”). Compare Portuguese and Spanish orla.
