Alteration, under the influence of orne, of Old French ordiere, inherited from Vulgar Latin *orbitaria, from Latin orbita.
Inherited from Old French oblier, from Vulgar Latin *oblītāre, frequentative of Latin oblīvīscor (via its past participle oblītus).

First attested in 1380, from Old French oïl (1100), from Vulgar Latin *hoc ille or by surface analysis a compound of Old French o (affirmative particle) and il (“he”). Partially cognate to Occitan òc (“yes”) and Catalan oi (“isn't it?”). See the Old French term for details.
Inherited from Old French orler, from Vulgar Latin *orulāre, from *orula, diminutive of Latin ora. Compare Italian orlare, Spanish orlar.

parole.significato: tool (something designed to aid in a task)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French outil, from Old French ostil, ustil, from Vulgar Latin *usitilium, derived from Latin ūtēnsilia.
Inherited from Middle French ouvert, from Old French overt, from Vulgar Latin *opertus, from Latin apertus. Doublet of apert.
Inherited from Old French overture, from Vulgar Latin *opertūra, from Latin apertūra. Doublet of aperture, a borrowing. Compare Catalan obertura.
From Old French ovraige, ovrage, from Vulgar Latin *operāticum, from Latin opera. Cognate to Bourguignon ovraige.
Inherited from Middle French ouvrir, from Old French ovrir, obrir, from Vulgar Latin *operīre, alteration of Classical Latin aperīre (“to open”). See also Italian oprire; Catalan obrir.

parole.significato: palate; upper surface inside the mouth
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French, from Vulgar Latin *palātium, an alteration of Latin palātum (“palate”) from the influence of palātium (“palace”).
Through Vulgar Latin, from Latin pelōris.
Inherited from Old French panel, inherited from Vulgar Latin *pannellus. Doublet of panel.
Inherited from Old French pantaisier/pantoisier, from Vulgar Latin pantasiare. Cognate with Old Occitan pantaizar/pantaissar/pantaiar, Sicilian pantasciari, Neapolitan pantasiari, Catalan pantaixar.
Inherited from Middle French paroistre, from Old French paroistre, pareistre, from Vulgar Latin *pārēscere, from Latin pārēre.
Inherited from Old French parchemin, from Vulgar Latin *pergamīnus, from Late Latin pergamēna.
From Vulgar Latin percursus, nominalised past participle of percurrere. Parcourir is a much later borrowing from percurrere.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *parmēsānus.

parole.significato: speech, language (the faculty of using spoken language to communicate or express thought, the usage of this faculty, an…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French parole, from Old French parole, inherited from Vulgar Latin *paraula, from Late Latin, from Latin parabola (“comparison; (later) speech”), from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ). Doublet of parabole and palabre.
Inherited from Middle French passer, from Old French passer, from Vulgar Latin *passāre, derived from Latin passus (“step”, noun).

Inherited from Middle French patois (“local dialect”), from Old French patois (“incomprehensible speech, rude language”), alteration (due to influence of the suffix -ois in words relating to nationalities and languages) of earlier *patoi, a deverbal of patoier (“to gesticulate, handle clumsily, paw”

From Middle French, from Old French pade, pate (“paw, foot of an animal”), from Vulgar Latin *patta (“paw, foot”), borrowed from Frankish *patta (“paw, sole of the foot”), from Proto-Germanic *pat-, *paþa- (“to walk, tread, go, step”), of uncertain origin and relation. Possibly from Proto-Indo-Europ
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *palpetra, variant of Latin palpebra.

parole.significato: to cobble, to pave with cobblestones or something similar
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French paver (“to pave, to cover”), from Vulgar Latin *pavāre (“to beat down, to smash”), from Latin pavīre (“to beat, strike, ram, tread down”).

Inherited from Middle French paintre, from Old French peintre, paintre, from the nominative case of Vulgar Latin *pinctor, from Classical Latin pictor (“painter”). Cf. also the Old French forms peintor, paintor, poentor, from the Vulgar Latin accusative *pinctorem.
Inherited from Old French peinture, from Vulgar Latin *pinctūra, alteration of the classical Latin pictūra, under the influence of the verb it's derived from, pingō.
From Old French pelote (“small ball”), from Vulgar Latin *pilotta, diminutive of Latin pila (“ball”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pendicāre, from Latin pendere (“hang”). Compare pendre.
From Vulgar Latin *pendita, nominalized feminine of *penditus, Vulgar Latin perfect participle (compare Classical Latin pēnsus) of pendere (“to hang”).
From Old French percier, from Vulgar Latin *pertusiāre, from Latin pertusus (“perforated”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerH-dʰh₁- (“to pierce, strike”). Compare Italian pertugiare.
Inherited from Old French percevoir, perceveir, from Vulgar Latin *percipēre, variant form of Classical Latin percipĕre (“to seize, to observe”).
Inherited from Old French petit, from Vulgar Latin pittitus (775; compare Latin pitinnus, pitulus). Compare Spanish pequeño.
Inherited from Old French peoros, from Vulgar Latin *pavōrōsum, derived from Latin pavōrem (“fear”, noun). By surface analysis, peur + -eux.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *piccus, from Latin pīcus.
From Vulgar Latin *pinnio, from Latin pinna.
With a change of suffix, from Old French piler, from Vulgar Latin *pilāre, from Latin pila.
From Old French pincel, from Vulgar Latin *penicellus, alteration of Latin pēnicillum.
From Vulgar Latin *pincio (acc. *pincionem) from Gaulish (compare Welsh pinc), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pingos (compare English finch). Compare Spanish pinzón, Italian pincione.

parole.significato: a French-Canadian term for an Imperial quart, equal to ¹⁄₄ of an Imperial gallon, 2 Imperial pints, 40 Imperial ounces…
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *pincta (“mark used to indicate level on vessels”), from Latin pictus (“painted”), from Latin pingō (“paint”, verb).
Inherited from Old French pissier, from Vulgar Latin *pīssiāre, of originally Germanic origin or more likely of echoic origin. Cognates include Catalan pixar, Italian pisciare, Romanian pișa.
From Vulgar Latin *pipa (“whistle, flute”), from Latin pipāre.
Inherited from Middle French piege, from Old French piege, from Vulgar Latin *pedicus, from Latin pedica, from pēs, pedis (“foot”).
Inherited from Middle French, from Vulgar Latin *peditalia (“foot soldier”). By surface analysis, pied (“foot”) + -aille (derogatory suffix). Compare piéton (“pedestrian”).
Inherited from Middle French plaider, from Old French plaidier, from plait, possibly corresponding to a Vulgar Latin *placitare, from Latin placitum. Cognate with English plead.
Inherited from Old French planche, from Vulgar Latin planca, contracted from palanca, from Latin phalanga, from Ancient Greek φάλαγξ (phálanx).
Inherited from Old French, from Vulgar Latin *plantionem, accusative of *plantio, from plantare.
Inherited from Middle French plat, from Old French plat, from Vulgar Latin *plattus, from Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús, “broad, flat”).
Inherited from Old French plovoir, from earlier pluveir, from Vulgar Latin *plovere (with a change in conjugation to *plovēre), from Classical Latin pluere.
From Old French plongier, from Vulgar Latin *plumbicāre, from Latin plumbum (“lead”).
From Old French pelote (“small ball”), from Vulgar Latin *pilotta, diminutive of Latin pila (“ball”).
From Middle French pluye, from Old French pluie, from Vulgar Latin *plo(v)ia.
Inherited from Old French plusors, from Vulgar Latin *plūsiōres, alteration of Late Latin plūriōres (by influence from plūs), from Latin plūres.
Inherited from Old French plovier, from Vulgar Latin *pluviārius, probably from Latin pluvia.

parole.significato: plaster, plaster of Paris (the building material)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French plâtre, plastre, from Old French plastre (first attested ca. 1165), from Vulgar Latin *plastrum (attested later in Medieval Latin plastrum), from Latin emplastrum, from Ancient Greek ἔμπλαστρον (émplastron, “daub; salve”). Doublet of piastre.

Inherited from Middle French poix, from Old French pois, peis, from Vulgar Latin *pēsum, from Latin pēnsum. Spelling influenced by Latin pondus with the same meaning; both ultimately from the root of pendō (“to weigh”). Doublet of pensum, which was borrowed.

Alteration of Old French poignal, poignel, from Vulgar Latin *pugnāle(m), from Latin pugnus (“fist”) (whence French poing), in the manner of manuālis. Compare Spanish puñal; Portuguese and Occitan punhal; Catalan punyal; Italian pugnale.
Inherited from Old French peire, from Vulgar Latin *pira, from the plural of Latin pirum, considered as a feminine singular.
Inherited from Old French perier, from Vulgar Latin *pirārius (cf. Medieval Latin pirarius), from Latin pirus. Reanalyzed as poire (“pear”) + -ier.
Inherited from Middle French poiré, from earlier peré (remodelled after poire), from Old French peré, from Vulgar Latin *pirātum. By surface analysis, poire (“pear”) + -é.
Inherited from Old French poitrine, peitrine, from Vulgar Latin *pectorīna, derived from Latin pectus. Gradually replaced pis, now meaning udder. Cognate with Spanish pretina (“waistband”).
Inherited from Old French puncel, from Vulgar Latin ponticellus, a variant of Classical Latin ponticulus, from pōns + -culus.

parole.significato: to stop carrying, to put down (something or somebody)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French poser, from Vulgar Latin pausāre < Latin pausāre, influenced in meaning by pōnō (especially its past participle positus). Compare Italian posare.

parole.significato: pot, jar, vase, tin, can, carton (a container of any of various materials)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French pot, from Old French pot (“pot”), from Vulgar Latin pottum, pottus (“pot, jar”), from Frankish *pott, from Proto-Germanic *puttaz (“pot, jar, tub”), from Proto-Indo-European *budn- (“a kind of vessel”). More at English pot.
Inherited from Old French, from Vulgar Latin pulla, feminine form of Latin pullus.

Inherited from Middle French poupée, from Old French poupee, popede (cf. also Medieval Latin *pupāta), or Vulgar Latin *puppa (with the French suffix -ée later added), ultimately from Latin pūpa (“girl; doll, puppet”). Borrowed into English as puppy and puppet, see those entries for more.
Inherited from Old French porrir, from Vulgar Latin *putrīre, from Latin putrēre, with inflexions taken from putrēscere.

Inherited from Old French porsivre, poursivre, porsuir, poursuire, porsivir, from Vulgar Latin *prosequere (attested in Vulgar or early Medieval Latin as prosevere and prosequire), from Latin prosequi. Most of the other Romance cognates (as well as the Old French parsivre, parsuivre) derived from th
Inherited from Old French pousiere, derived from pous, from Vulgar Latin *pulvus, neuter form derived from Latin pulvis m.
From Old French poutre, probably from apocope of an earlier *poutrelle, from a Vulgar Latin *pultrella < pulitrella from the feminine of Latin pullitrum, ultimately from pullus (“colt, youngling”).

Inherited from Middle French povoir, from Old French povoir, pooir, from earlier Old French poeir, podeir, from Vulgar Latin potēre, regularization of Latin posse. The /-v-/ was eventually added, after the loss of the intervocalic dental, to break hiatus. The archaic 1SG present indicative puis is f
Inherited from Old French praerie, from Vulgar Latin *prataria, from Latin prātum (“meadow”) + -aria. See also pré and -erie.
Inherited from Old French prochain, from Vulgar Latin *propeānus, derived from Latin prope (“near”). Cognate with Sardinian probianu.
Inherited from Old French prune, from Vulgar Latin *prūna, feminine singular formed from the neutral plural of Latin prūnum, from Ancient Greek προῦμνον (proûmnon).

parole.significato: near (a time or a place); close (to a time or a place)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French prés (“closely”), from Vulgar Latin *pressō, from Latin presse (“narrow, short”) and pressus (“concise”), from premō (“to press, push, condense”). Cognate with Italian presso and Sicilian pressu.
Inherited from Old French prisure, from Vulgar Latin *prēnsūra, derived from Latin prehēnsum.
Rebracketing of Vulgar Latin *asperella, from asper (“rough”).

From Middle French prosne (“homily”), from Old French prodne (“grating around the altar, in front of which the priest stood during homily”), from Vulgar Latin *protinum, dissimilation of protirum, from Classical Latin prothyra, from Ancient Greek πρόθυρα (próthura, “vestibule”).

Inherited from Old French puir (with a change in conjugation), from Vulgar Latin *putīre, from Classical Latin pūtēre (also with a change in conjugation), present active infinitive of pūteō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *puH-.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *postius, a comparative of Latin post (“after”). Compare Portuguese pois, Spanish pues, Italian poi, and Romanian apoi (archaic păi).

parole.significato: bug, stinkbug; true bug (a member of order Heteroptera)
parole.testo: From the feminine of punais (“having a foul odor”), from Vulgar Latin *pūtināsius, from Latin puteō + nāsus, based on nāriputēns.

Inherited from Old French putain, originally the oblique case of pute (“dirty woman”) formed with the suffix -ain, from Vulgar Latin pūtta, from Latin pūta (“girl”). Compare with salope, Italian puttana, Spanish puta.

From Old French pute (nominative singular of putain) – perhaps from:. * a Vulgar Latin *pūtta, from a supposed Latin *puta (“girl”), female form of putus (“boy”) (a hapax legomenon of dubious reading) * from the feminine form of put (“stinking, fetid”), from Latin pūtidus (“stinking”), therefore eff
Blend of pâtis + pasquier, from Vulgar Latin *pascuarium.

Inherited from Old French pasticier (“make pâté, make pastry”), from an unattested noun *pastitz (compare Old Occitan pastis, pastitz, Italian pasticcio), from a Vulgar Latin *pastīcius, from Late Latin pasta (“paste”), from Ancient Greek παστά (pastá, “barley porridge”), from παστός (pastós, “salte
Inherited from Old French penil, from Vulgar Latin *pectinī̆culum, diminutive of pecten (“pubic hair, comb”).

Inherited from Old French pipie, from Vulgar Latin *pippīta, alteration of Latin pītuīta (“mucus”). The form with a geminated *-pp- also underlies the Germanic borrowings (German Pips, Dutch and English pip). Other Romance shows simple -p- (e.g. Italian pipita, Portuguese pevide) attested as Medieva
Inherited from Old French pepin, and according to Etymonline, probably from a root like Vulgar Latin *pép(p)-, an expressive creation used to convey smallness.
Inherited from Old French peril, from Vulgar Latin *periclu(m), syncopated form of Latin perīculum.
Inherited from Middle French pesche, from Old French pesche, from Vulgar Latin *pessica (cf. Medieval Latin pesca), from Late Latin persica, from Latin persicum. Doublet of persique.
Inherited from Middle French queu, cueue, from Old French cue, coe, from Vulgar Latin cōda, variant of Latin cauda. Doublet of coda.
Inherited from Old French keuz, from Vulgar Latin *cotis, from Latin cos, cotis. Cognate with Italian cote.

parole.significato: people, mainly young, who engage in antisocial behaviour; rabble, riffraff; rascals
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French rascaille (“outcast, rabble”), perhaps from rasque (“mud, filth, scab, dregs”), from Vulgar Latin *rasicō (“to scrape”). Cognate with English rascal.

parole.significato: ridge between furrows, balk (an unplowed strip of land)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French roie, from Vulgar Latin [Term?], probably from Gaulish *ricā (“furrow”), from Proto-Celtic *ɸrikā (“furrow”, compare Old Irish rech).

Inherited from Middle French railler, from Vulgar Latin *raglāre < *ragulāre, from Late Latin ragō (“to bray”) (whence Old French raire (“to shout, said of deer”), réer (“to shout, said of deer”), Romanian rage (“to scream, said of people or especially animals”); attested once directly in a 10th-cen

From Old French roisner + -ure, from Vulgar Latin *rucina, borrowed from Gaulish *rucina, in turn borrowed from Ancient Greek ῥῠκάνη (rhŭkánē, “plane, a carpenter's tool”). According to Beekes, the word is likely of Pre-Greek origin, and probably the source for Latin runcīna.

parole.significato: small branch (woody part of a tree arising from the trunk and usually dividing)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French ramel, from Vulgar Latin *ramellus, from Latin rāmus, from Proto-Indo-European *wréh₂ds (“root”).
From Middle French rancune, from Old French rancune, dissimilated from rancure, from Vulgar Latin *rancura, from Latin rancor.
Inherited from Old French raser, from Vulgar Latin *rāsāre, a frequentative verb formed from Latin rāsus, past participle of rādō. Compare Italian rasare.

parole.significato: strikeout, crossing-out (act of crossing out a word to indicate deletion)
parole.testo: From Old French rasture, from Vulgar Latin *rasitōria, from rāsitō, frequentative of rādō (“I scrape”).
Inherited from Old French ravir, from Vulgar Latin *rapīre, from Latin rapiō, from Proto-Italic *rapjō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁r̥p-i-, from *h₁rep- (“to snatch”).
From Vulgar Latin *rebursus, alteration of reburrus (“with bristing hair”) by analogy with reversus.
Inherited from Middle French recevoir, from Old French recevoir, from Vulgar Latin *recipēre, from Latin recipiō. Cognate with English receive through borrowing, see there for more.
Alteration of Old French refrait, past participle of the verb refraindre (based on the verb's infinitive), itself from Vulgar Latin *refrangere, from Latin refringere.
Inherited from Old French refuser, from Vulgar Latin *refūsāre, a blend of Latin refūtāre and recūsāre.

parole.significato: to fill, to fill up (make full)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French remplir, from Old French remplir, from re- + emplir, which is itself from Vulgar Latin *implīre, from Latin implēre.
From Vulgar Latin *renegāre, from Latin re- + negāre. Compare Italian rinnegare and Spanish renegar.
Inherited from Middle French repentir, from Vulgar Latin *repaenitīre, from Late Latin paenitīre, from Classical Latin paenitēre. Compare English repent.
From Middle French requeste, from Old French requeste, from Vulgar Latin *requaesita, from Latin requīsīta.
Inherited from Middle French retenir, from Old French retenir, from Vulgar Latin *retenīre, from Latin retinēre, from re- + teneō (“to hold”).

parole.significato: to trim, to snip, to cut, to crop (a picture)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French rooignier, redognier, reoignier, from a Vulgar Latin *retundiāre, alteration of *rotundiāre, from Latin rotundus. Compare Old Occitan redonhar.

Inherited from Middle French rognon, roignon, from Old French roignon, rognon, from Vulgar Latin *rēniōnem, *rēniōnem, from Latin rēn (“kidney”). Cognate with Norman rignon, Spanish riñón, Occitan renhon. See also French rein and -on.

Inherited from Old French romanz (“common language (as opposed to Latin)”), from Vulgar Latin romanicē (“in the way of the Romans (as opposed to the Franks)”), from Latin rōmānicus, from Latin rōmānus. The meaning “common language” changed into “book in common language” and then into “adventure nove
Inherited from Old French roissier, probably from Vulgar Latin *rustiare, from *rustia, from Late Latin rustum, or less likely from Vulgar Latin *ruptiāre, from Latin ruptus, from rumpō.

parole.significato: dew (moisture in the air that settles on plants, etc)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French rosee, rousee, rosede, from a Vulgar Latin *rōsāta (“dew, mist”), from Latin rōs (“dew, moisture”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rṓs.

Inherited from Old French reoïlle, from Vulgar Latin *robicla, from syncopation of Latin *robicula, a diminutive of Latin rōbīgō (“rust”) + -cula (from -culus (suffix forming diminutives)). Rōbīgō is derived from rōbus (a variant of rūfus (“red, reddish”)) + -īgō (suffix forming nouns usually denoti
Inherited from Old French ru, riu, from Vulgar Latin *rius, from Latin rīvus (“brook, small stream”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃rih₂wós (from *h₃reyh₂- (“to flow; to move, set in motion”) + *-wós).

parole.significato: to kick with its hind legs
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *rutāre, based on the supine stem of Classical Latin ruō.

From Old French ruissel, from Vulgar Latin *rivuscellum (“brook, stream”), from Latin *rīvusculum (“creek, rivulet”) + -ellum (“-elle: forming diminutives”), from rīvus (“rivulet”) + -usculum (“-cule: forming diminutives”). Compare Italian ruscello.

Inherited from Middle French râper < rasper, from Old French rasper, from Vulgar Latin *raspāre (“to scrape; rake”), from Frankish *hraspōn, from Proto-Germanic *hraspōną, a derivative of Proto-Germanic *hrespaną (“to tear”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)krebʰ- (“to turn; bend; shrink”). Romance cog
Inherited from Old French, from Vulgar Latin sablum, from Latin sabulum, alternative form of sabulō. Compare sablon, which was used more often in Old French. Compare Italian sabbia, Occitan sabla.

Inherited from Old French, from a Vulgar Latin root *salāre, from a change in conjugation of Latin salīre (“to salt”), from sal. Compare Italian salare, Romanian săra, Spanish, Portuguese, and Catalan salar.

Inherited from Old French samedi, from Vulgar Latin *sambatum and *sambatī diēs, from Latin Sabbatī diēs, variant of diēs Sabbatī (“day of the Sabbath”), from sabbatum, from Ancient Greek σάββατον (sábbaton) (Modern Greek: Σάββατο (Sávvato)), from Hebrew שַׁבָּת (shabát). See also sabbat, chabbat.
Inherited from Old French sanc, from Vulgar Latin sanguem, alteration of Latin sanguinem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁sh₂-én-, oblique stem of *h₁ésh₂r̥ (“blood”).
Inherited from Old French cengle, from Vulgar Latin *cingla, from Late Latin cingula, from Latin cingulum.

parole.significato: wild boar (specifically, a full-grown wild boar)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French sengler, from Vulgar Latin *singlāris, inherited from Latin singulāris (porcus) (literally “solitary pig”), with later substitution of the suffix -ier for -er. Compare Occitan singlar, Catalan senglar, Italian cinghiale, Friulian cenglâr. Doublet of singulier.

Inherited from Old French sangloit, singlot, from Vulgar Latin *singluttus, a blend of gluttīre (“to swallow”) + Latin singultus (“a hiccup”). Compare Catalan sanglot, Italian singhiozzo, and Occitan sanglòt.
Inherited from Old French sangloter, from Vulgar Latin *singluttāre, from Latin singultāre, with influence from gluttīre. Compare Italian singhiozzare, Occitan and Catalan sanglotar.
From earlier cercelle, from Vulgar Latin *cercedula, variant form of Latin querquedula.
Inherited from Old French sause, from Vulgar Latin *salsa, nominal use of the feminine of Latin salsus (“salted”), perfect participle of saliō (“to salt”), from sāl.
From Old French saumastre, from Vulgar Latin *salmaster, alteration of Latin salmacidus (“salty and bitter”), from salgama (“salted pickle”) + acidus (“bitter”). Doublet of saumache.
Inherited from Old French sauvage, salvage, from Vulgar Latin salvāticus, from Latin silvāticus, from silva (“forest”).

Inherited from Old French savoir/eir, from Vulgar Latin *sapēre, from Latin sapĕre. Comments The now-obsolete spelling sçavoir owes its ⟨ç⟩ to the Latin scīre (“to know”), which was long assumed to be the etymon of the French verb. The 1SG present indicative sais comes from Old French sai < Vulgar L

Inherited from Middle French sceller, from Old French seeler, from Vulgar Latin *sigellāre, from Latin sigillāre (“to seal”), from sigillum (“seal”). See sceau. Compare also Catalan segellar, Spanish sellar, Portuguese selar, Italian suggellare.
Inherited from Old French seel, from Vulgar Latin *sitellus, from sitella (“kind of urn”).
Inherited from Old French secors, socors, from Vulgar Latin *succursum, from Latin succursus. Compare Italian soccorso, Portuguese socorro and Spanish socorro.
Inherited from Middle French sarge, from Old French sarge, from Vulgar Latin *sarica, from Latin sērica, ultimately from the Ancient Greek σηρῐκός (sērĭkós, “silken”).

parole.significato: billhook, pruning hook, sickle (agricultural implement often with a curved or hooked end to the blade used for pruning…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French serpe, from Vulgar Latin *sarpa, from Latin sarpō. Compare Medieval Latin sarpa.
Inherited from Old French sarpilliere, probably from Vulgar Latin *sirpiculāria, derived from Latin scirpiculus (from scirpus (“bullrush”)).
Inherited from Old French serrer, from Vulgar Latin *serrāre (“close, shut”), from Late Latin serāre (“fasten, bolt”), from Latin sera (“bolt, crossbar”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *solium, a blend of Latin solum (“flat ground”) + solea (“flat object, sandal”). Compare Italian soglia.
Inherited from Old French sevrer, inherited from Vulgar Latin *sēperāre, apophonic form of Latin sēparāre. Doublet of séparer, a borrowing.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sitellus, from Latin sitella.

parole.significato: sir, Mr., lord; title of respect for a man
parole.testo: From the oblique case of Old French sire (see also French sire), from Vulgar Latin *seior (“lord, elder”), from Latin senior (“older, elder”) (whence also seigneur, from the accusative form), from senex (“old”). Cognate with Spanish señor, Italian signore, etc. Also a doublet of senior and sire.

Inherited from Old French sifler (later orthographically influenced by souffler), from Vulgar Latin *sīfilāre, probably an Osco-Umbrian influenced variant of Latin sībilāre (compare Spanish chiflar, Friulian sivilâ). Compare also the variant northern Old French dialectal form sufler (whence Norman s

parole.significato: sire (term of respect) (Still used in at least partly French-speaking kingdoms such as Belgium or Canada as a form of a…
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French sire (nominative form), from Vulgar Latin *seior (used as a term of address), a contracted form of Latin senior (compare French seigneur, derived from the accusative form), perhaps influenced by maior. Doublet of seigneur, senior, and sieur.
From Vulgar Latin *soccus, a word borrowed from Gaulish, from Proto-Celtic *sukkos (literally “pig's snout”) (compare Middle Irish socc, Welsh swch (“plowshare”)), from Proto-Indo-European *suH-.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sola, from Latin solea.
Inherited from Middle French soleil, from Old French soleil, from Vulgar Latin *sōliculus, diminutive of Latin sōl (“sun”), from Proto-Indo-European *sóh₂wl̥.

Inherited from Old French sumeil, from Vulgar Latin *somniclum < *somniculum, from Latin somnus (“sleep”) + -culus (diminutive suffix), from Proto-Italic *swepnos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swépnos.
From sommeil + -er. Cf. also Vulgar Latin *somniculāre, whence also Italian sonnecchiare.

parole.significato: sommelier, wine steward (a person who is in charge of the wine cellar in a restaurant)
parole.testo: From somme + -ier; ultimately from bête de somme; somme is from Vulgar Latin *salma, from Latin sagma (“packsaddle”).

parole.significato: his, her, their, its (used to qualify masculine nouns and before a vowel)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French son, from Old French son, from Vulgar Latin sum, a reduced/atonic variant of suus, suum, from Proto-Italic *sowos, from Proto-Indo-European *sewos, from *swé (“self”).

Inherited from Middle French souche, from Old French çoche, from Vulgar Latin *tsucca, from Gaulish *tsukka, from Proto-Germanic *stukkaz (“stock; stump”). Cognate with Catalan and Spanish soca, Sicilian zuccu. More at English stock.

parole.significato: sudden (happening quickly and with little or no warning)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French sodein, from Vulgar Latin *subitānus, from Latin subitāneus (“sudden”), from subitus.
From Old French suffraitus, from suffraite + -us. suffraite is from Vulgar Latin *suffracta, feminine singular of the perfect passive participle of *suffrangō.
Inherited from Old French sofrir, from Vulgar Latin *sufferīre, from Latin sufferre.

Inherited from Middle French souhaiter, itself (with /t/ through influence of the noun souhait) from Old French sohaidier, from Gallo-Roman Vulgar Latin *subhaitare (“to vow with little commitment”, literally “under-promise”), a hybrid of Latin subtus (“under”) + Frankish *haitan (“to order, promise

Alteration of Old French suslegier (probably under the influence of solacier (“to solace”) and soulas) from Vulgar Latin *subleviāre, from Latin sublevāre (“to lift up, to raise; to lighten”), from sub- (“from under”) + levō (“to raise, to lift up”).
Inherited from Middle French soubrire (silent b), from Old French sorrirre, from Vulgar Latin *subrīdĕre, from Latin subrīdēre.

Inherited from Middle French souris, from Old French soris, soriz, from Vulgar Latin *sōrīcem, alteration of the Classical Latin sōricem (“shrew”). The computing sense is a semantic loan from English mouse.
Inherited from Middle French soustenir, from Old French sustenir, soustenir, from Vulgar Latin *sustenīre, from Latin sustinēre. Asynchronically analyzable as sou- + tenir.
Inherited from Old French soverain, from Vulgar Latin *superānus, from Latin super. Compare Italian sovrano; Galician, Portuguese, and Spanish soberano.
Inherited from Old French suite, from earlier siute, from Vulgar Latin *sequita, (instead of classical secūta), as the feminine past participle of *sequere, from Latin sequi.
Inherited from Middle French suyvre, from Old French sivre, siure, segre, from Vulgar Latin *sequere of deponent Latin sequī.
Inherited from Old French secherece, from Vulgar Latin *siccāricia, from Latin siccus (“dry”). By surface analysis, sèche + -eresse.

Inherited from Old French sojorner by vowel dissimilation (first ‘o’ → ‘é’), inherited from Vulgar Latin *subdiurnāre, from Latin sub- (“under, a little over”) + Late Latin diurnus (“lasting for a day”).

Inherited from Middle French tache, from Old French tache, taiche, taje (“mark, spot, stain”), from Vulgar Latin *tacca, *tecca, from Gothic 𐍄𐌰𐌹𐌺𐌽𐍃 (taikns, “mark, sign”), from Proto-Germanic *taiknaz, *taikną (“sign, mark”), from Proto-Indo-European *deyḱ- (“to show”). Influenced by forms related t
Inherited from Old French tachier, techier, from Vulgar Latin *tagicare, from Latin taxāre (“to feel, touch”). Doublet of taxer.
Inherited from Old French taillëiz, from Vulgar Latin *taliātīcius, from Latin taliāre (“cut”). By surface analysis, tailler + -is.
Inherited from Old French tencier, from Vulgar Latin *tentiāre, from Latin tentus, the past participle of tendō.
Inherited from Old French täun, tahon, toon, from Vulgar Latin *tabōnem, from Latin tabānus (“gadfly, horsefly”). Compare Norman taon, Franco-Provençal tôna, Romanian tăun.
From Vulgar Latin *tempula, from Latin tempora, originally an accusative plural form of tempus.
From Vulgar Latin tenacula, taken as a feminine singular of Latin tenaculum, from teneō. Compare Occitan and Portuguese tenalha.
Inherited from Old French terrain, terrein, from Vulgar Latin *terranum, from Latin terrēnum.
Loaned from Vulgar Latin *terrificare, from Latin terrārī + faciō, facere (“make”).

parole.significato: Area of natural land considered in terms of agriculture.
parole.testo: From late Old French tieroir, terroir, inherited from Vulgar Latin *terratorium, from Classical Latin territorium, from Latin terra (“land”). Doublet of territoire, which was borrowed.

parole.significato: little tuna (fish of the Euthynnus genus)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French tonine, from Vulgar Latin *thunnīna, from thunnus (“tuna”) + -īna (derivational suffix).
Inherited from Old French tilluel, from Vulgar Latin *tiliolus, from Latin tilia. Cf. also Old French til.
From Vulgar Latin *tinnitāre, frequentative of Latin tinniō.
Inherited from Old French petit, from Vulgar Latin pittitus (775; compare Latin pitinnus, pitulus), possibly from Celtic or Frankish (cf. petit).
From Middle French tirer, from Old French tirer, from Vulgar Latin *tīrāre.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tītiāre, from Latin tītiāre (“firebrand”) (whence tison). Compare the related term attiser.
Inherited from Old French tondre, from Vulgar Latin *tondĕre, variant of Latin tondēre, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tend-, from *temh₂- (“to cut”).

parole.significato: a feudal tax paid by stallholders at a fair or market
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French tonliu, tolniu, from Vulgar Latin *tolōnēum, variant of Latin telōnēum (“tollbooth, custom house”), from Ancient Greek τελωνεῖον (telōneîon, “custom house”). Influenced by lieu due to folk etymology.

parole.significato: torch (stick with flame at one end)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French torche, from Vulgar Latin *torca, from torqua, Classical Latin torques, from the verb torqueō (“to twist; to turn”).
Inherited from Old French tordre, tortre, from Vulgar Latin *torcĕre, from Latin torquēre.
From Old French torke, northern variant of torche, from Vulgar Latin *torca, ultimately from the same source as etymology 1.

parole.significato: tangle, maze of threads of hemp, silk, wax etc.
parole.testo: From Middle French tortis, tourtis, from the past passive participle tortis, tortiz etc., based on a Vulgar Latin *torticium from tortus.

Inherited from Middle French toucher, from Old French tochier, from Vulgar Latin *toccāre, *tuccāre (“to strike; to touch”), probably of Germanic origin, from Frankish *tukkōn (“to hit, bump, contact”); or onomatopoetic.
Substantivization of Old French tornëiz (“revolving, turning”), from Vulgar Latin *tornātīcius, from Latin tornāre (“to turn”). By surface analysis, tourner + -is.

Inherited from Middle French tout, from Old French tot, from Vulgar Latin tōttus, alteration (likely via expressive gemination) of Latin tōtus. Compare Catalan tot, Italian tutto, Portuguese todo, Romanian tot, Spanish todo.

parole.significato: to draw or plot (a diagram), to trace out
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French tracier, from Vulgar Latin *tractiāre, from Latin tractum the past participle of trahō.

parole.significato: a cable along which a ferry is pulled
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French, from a Vulgar Latin *tragla, contraction of Latin tragula.
Inherited from Middle French train, from Old French train, from the verb trahiner (“to pull, drag”) (whence traîner).

Inherited from Middle French travailler, from Old French travailler (“to toil, suffer, torment”), from Vulgar Latin *tripāliāre (“to torture”), derived from Late Latin tripālium (“torture instrument”), from Latin tripālis (“having three stakes”).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin traversus, from Latin trānsversus. Doublet of transverse. Compare Italian traverso.
From Vulgar Latin traversa, feminine of traversus.
Inherited from Old French traïner, from Vulgar Latin *tragīnāre, from *tragere (see traire), from Latin trahere (“to pull”). Compare Italian trascinare, Catalan traginar, Spanish trajinar.
From Vulgar Latin *trilicius < Latin trilix.
Inherited from Old French tresce, of uncertain origin; possibly from Vulgar Latin *trichia < Ancient Greek. Compare Italian treccia, Sicilian trizza.
Inherited from Old French treuil, from Vulgar Latin *troculum, from Latin torculum.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *trunca, feminine form of truncus (“tree trunk”) (→ tronc).
From Old French trons, from Vulgar Latin *trunceus, from Latin truncus.

parole.significato: murky, turbid, muddy, thick, clouded, cloudy; not clear
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French troble, probably from a Vulgar Latin *turbulus (with metathesis), itself perhaps an alteration of Latin turbidus with influence from turbulentus; cf. also turbula. Compare Catalan tèrbol, Romanian tulbure.
With metathesis, from Vulgar Latin *torsāre, from *torsus, variant of Classical Latin tortus, past participle of torqueō.
Inherited from Old French tresfle, from Vulgar Latin *trifolum, from Latin trifolium, calque of Ancient Greek τρίφυλλον (tríphullon). Or taken from the Greek itself. Compare Old French trefeuil.

parole.significato: to feel (touch lightly, to sense consistency or temperature)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French taster, from Vulgar Latin *tastāre, contraction of *taxitō, frequentative of Late Latin taxāre (“touch repeatedly”), from Latin taxus. Compare English taste.

From Old French tost, from Vulgar Latin tostum, from the neuter of Latin tostus (“toasted”), later meaning "hotly, promptly" in Vulgar Latin. Cognate to Italian tosto, Franco-Provençal toût, Catalan tost, Occitan tost, Walloon toist, Ladin tosc.

Inherited from Old French vaissele, veissele, from Vulgar Latin vāscella, from the neuter plural of Late Latin vāscellum, diminutive of Latin vāsculum, diminutive of vās (“vessel”). Compare Catalan vaixella, Spanish vajilla.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin vannāre, from Latin vannere, vannō.
Inherited from Old French vanter, from Vulgar Latin or Late Latin vānitāre, from Latin vānus or vānitās. Compare Italian vantare.

parole.significato: to wallow (to roll one's body, or a part of it, in the mud or something of similar texture)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *volūtulāre (“to tumble over”), from Latin volūtum, from the verb volvō.
Inherited from Middle French veiller, veigler, from Old French veillier, veiller, from Vulgar Latin *viglāre, contracted from Latin vigilāre. Compare the borrowed doublet vigiler.
Inherited from Middle French venin, from Old French venim, from Vulgar Latin *venīmen, from Early Medieval Latin venīnum, from Classical Latin venēnum.

From Old French verdir (12th c.), possibly inherited from Vulgar Latin *vir(i)dire, an alteration of Classical Latin viridēscere. Compare Italian inverdire, archaic Spanish enverdir (alongside enverdecer), Romanian înverzi. Equivalent to vert + -ir (the -t in vert being due to final devoicing).
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *viridizāre.
From vert (“green”) + -ure (noun-forming suffix), or from Vulgar Latin *virdūra.
Inherited from Middle French vergier, from Old French vergier, from Vulgar Latin *virdiariu, syncopated form of Latin viridiārium, variant of viridārium, from viridis.
Inherited from Old French vergogne, vergoigne, inherited from Vulgar Latin *verecunnia, from Latin verēcundia. Doublet of vérécondie, an obsolete Renaissance borrowing.
Inherited from Middle French vermeil, from Old French vermeil, syncopated form of Latin vermiculus (“little worm”).
From Vulgar Latin *vermicellus, alteration of vermiculus (“small worm”), from vermis (“worm”). Doublet of vermicelle.
Backformation from Middle French verroux, from the nominative-singular/accusative-plural of Old French veroil, from Vulgar Latin *verruculum, from Latin vericulum, diminutive of verū.

parole.significato: widower (a man whose wife has died and who has not remarried)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French, from Latin viduus, through a Vulgar Latin *viduvus.
Uncertain; possibly from a Vulgar Latin derivative of Latin volare or volvo; or, possibly from aveugle.
Inherited from Old French vaüve, veve, vedve, from Vulgar Latin *viduva, from Latin vidua.

Inherited from Old French viande, from Vulgar Latin *vīvanda, alteration of Latin vīvenda, from the neuter plural form of vīvendus, from vīvere (“to live”). Compare English viand, Italian vivanda, Portuguese vivenda, Spanish vivienda.
From Old French vuit, from Vulgar Latin *vocitum. The modern French form is due to generalisation of the feminine (Old French vuide) and assimilation vui- → vi-.
From Middle French vuider, from Old French vuidier, from Vulgar Latin *vocitāre, from Vulgar Latin *vocitum, ultimately connected to Latin vacuus.

Inherited from Middle French vigne, from Old French vigne, from Vulgar Latin vinia, from Latin vīnea (“vines in a vineyard”), from vīneus (“related to wine”), derived from vīnum (“wine”), from Proto-Italic *wīnom, from Proto-Indo-European *wóyh₁nom (“vine, wine”).
From Vulgar Latin *viriola, diminutive of viria (“bracelet”).
Inherited from Old French voile, veile, veille, from Vulgar Latin *vēla, from the plural of Latin vēlum, from Proto-Indo-European.
Inherited from Old French vomir, from Vulgar Latin *vomīre, from Latin vomere.
Inherited from Old French voloir, voleir, from Vulgar Latin volēre, regularized from Latin velle.
Inherited from Old French vosoir, from Vulgar Latin *volsorium, from *volsus, from Latin volvō (“to roll”).

Inherited from Old French volte, from Vulgar Latin *volta < *volvita or *volŭta, for Latin volūta, from the feminine of volūtus, perfect passive participle of volvō. Compare Italian volta; cf. Portuguese abóbada and Portuguese abóbeda, cf. also Spanish bóveda.
Inherited from Old French verille, ve(d)ille, from Vulgar Latin *vĭtīcula, from Late Latin vītīcula, from Classical Latin vītĭcula.
Past participle of voir. Inherited from Old French veü, from earlier vedüt, possibly corresponding to a Vulgar Latin *vidūtus in place of Latin vīsus. Compare Italian veduto, Romanian văzut.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ad poenam. Compare Italian appena, etc.
Inherited from Middle French âge, from Old French aage, eage, edage, from Vulgar Latin *aetāticum. The Old French forms displaced eé, the direct reflex of Latin aetātem.
From Old French astre, from Vulgar Latin *astracum, from Ancient Greek ὄστρακον (óstrakon, “potsherd”). Cognate with Galician ástrago.

From Middle French and Old French ça, from Vulgar Latin *ecce hāc. Compare Portuguese cá, Spanish acá. The grave accent now serves to distinguish it from ça (“that”). However, çà was already widely spelt thus before ça became common in writing, and in fact the accent was formerly also found for the
Inherited from Old French esbahir, esbaier, from Vulgar Latin *exbatāre, from Early Medieval Latin batāre.

Inherited from Middle French esblouir, from Old French esbleuir (“to dazzle”), from Vulgar Latin *exblaudō (“to dazzle”, verb), from ex- + *blaudō (“to overwhelm, to make someone weak”, verb), from Frankish *blōthijan, *blauthijan (“to overcome, make weak”), from Proto-Germanic *blauþijaną (“to make

The Vocabolario Etimologico of Pianigiani gives Vulgar Latin *excarptāre, formed with the supine Latin *excarptum of Latin *excarpāre or Latin excerpō (“choose, select”). At the same
Inherited from Old French eschangier, from Vulgar Latin *excambiāre (from Latin ex with Late Latin cambiāre).
Inherited from Middle French eschapper, from Old French eschaper, from Vulgar Latin *excappāre, a verb based on Late Latin cappa (“cloak”). Doublet of escaper.

Inherited from Middle French eschauffer, from Old French eschaufer, eschalfer, from Vulgar Latin *excalfāre, from Latin excal(e)facere, from ex + cal(e)facere. Ultimately related to échauder (cognate and synonym of English "scald").

parole.significato: to befall, to happen by chance
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French escheoir, from Vulgar Latin *excadēre (“fall out”), from Latin ex- + cadere.
Inherited from Old French esclairer, from Vulgar Latin *exclāriō, *exclāriāre, from Latin exclārāre, from ex- + clārō.
Compare Occitan esclòp, from Vulgar Latin scloppus.
Inherited from Old French esclore, from Vulgar Latin *exclaudere, remodelled from Latin exclūdere. Doublet of the borrowing exclure. Compare Piedmontese s-ciòde.

parole.significato: to dismiss, to get rid of (someone)
parole.testo: From an alteration, through the influence of conduire, of Old French escondire, itself from a Vulgar Latin *excondīcere, from Latin ex- + condīcere.

Inherited from Old French escrivain, from Vulgar Latin *scrībānem, from Latin scrība, with altered declension. Compare Occitan escrivan, Catalan escrivà, Italian scrivano, Spanish escribano. Doublet of scribe, a borrowing.

parole.significato: wild rosebush (either sweetbriar or dog rose)
parole.testo: From Middle French [Term?], from Old French aiglantier, eglenter, eglentier, from aiglant (“wild rosebush”) + -ier, with the first element derived from an apparent Vulgar Latin *aquilentum, an irregular derivative of Latin aculeus (“sting, prickle”) + -ulentum (“full of”), possibly a substantivized

Inherited from Middle French eglise, from Old French eglise, esglise, from Vulgar Latin *eclesia, from Latin ecclēsia, from Ancient Greek ἐκκλησία (ekklēsía, “gathering”). * Cognate with Catalan església, Italian chiesa, Portuguese igreja, Spanish iglesia
Inherited from Middle French eslire, from Old French eslire, from Vulgar Latin *exlegere, from Latin ēligere. Compare (obsolete) Spanish esleír, Italian scegliere.

Inherited from Old French esmeralde, esmeragde, from Vulgar Latin *smaralda, *smaraldus, *smaraudus, variant of Latin smaragdus (“emerald”), from Ancient Greek σμάραγδος (smáragdos), μάραγδος (máragdos, “emerald”), from a Semitic language.

Inherited from Middle French esmoy, from Old French esmai (“confusion, agitation caused by fear”), from esmaier (“to worry, scare, vex, dismay”), from Vulgar Latin *exmagare (“to deprive (someone) of strength, to disable”), from ex- + *magare (“to enable, empower”), from Proto-Germanic *maginą, *mag
Inherited from Middle French esmouvoir, from Old French esmouvoir, esmovoir, esmoveir, from Vulgar Latin *exmovēre, from Latin ēmovēre. Compare Italian smuovere.
Inherited from Old French espancier, from a Vulgar Latin *expandicāre, from Latin expandere.
Inherited from Old French espargnier, from Vulgar Latin sparāniāre (attested in the Reichenau Glossary), from Frankish *sparanjan, from Proto-West Germanic *sparēn (compare English spare).
Inherited from Old French esparpeillier, of uncertain origin; perhaps from a Vulgar Latin *disparpaliare, from dispār + palea + -are or dispellō (“to scatter”).

Inherited from Middle French espaule, from Old French espalle, from Vulgar Latin *spatla, from Late Latin spathula (“flat, broad piece”), itself the diminutive of Latin spatha (“straight sword”) (whence French épée (“sword”)). Doublet of spatule, a learned borrowing.

parole.significato: to spy on, keep an eye on, watch
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French espier, from Old French espier, from Vulgar Latin *spiāre (compare Italian spiare; Spanish, Portuguese, and Catalan espiar), from Frankish *spehōn, from Proto-Germanic *spehōną (“to spy”), from Proto-Indo-European *speḱ- (“to look”). Cognate with Middle Dutch spien (“to

parole.significato: pin (small device, made of drawn-out steel wire with one end sharpened and the other flattened or rounded into a head,…
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *spingula, a cross between Late Latin spīnula and spīcula. Cognate with Neapolitan spingula.
Inherited from Middle French esplucher, from Old French espeluchier, from Vulgar Latin *expiluc(i)cāre, ultimately from Latin pilāre (“remove hair”). Compare Occitan espelucar, Catalan espellucar.
Inherited from Middle French esponge, from Old French espoinge (cf. also variant espoigne), from Vulgar Latin *sponga, from Latin spongia, from Ancient Greek σπογγιά (spongiá).

Inherited from Old French espoenter, from Vulgar Latin *expaventāre, derived from the present participle of Classical Latin expaveō. Compare Occitan, Catalan, Spanish, and Portuguese espantar, Italian spaventare, also Romanian înspăimânta.
From a variant of Old French escarrer, from Vulgar Latin *exquadrāre, from Latin quadrus, quadra.

Inherited from Old French esquarre (“square”), from Vulgar Latin *exquadra, deverbal of *exquadrō, exquadrāre (whence French équarrir), from Latin quadrus, quadra. Compare Italian squadra. Doublet of escadre and square.

Inherited from Old French airable, from older arable, from Gallic Vulgar Latin or Late Latin acerābulus, from Latin acer (“maple”) + Gaulish *aballo- (“apple-tree”). Compare Old Irish ficabull (“fig-tree”), Welsh criafol (“mountain-ash”).

parole.significato: to make watertight, to stop water from flowing
parole.testo: Inherited from Old French estanchier, of uncertain origin: possibly from a Vulgar Latin *stanticāre < *stanticus < Latin stantem. Compare Italian stanco, stancare, Spanish estancar.

parole.significato: lowest water level (of a river course)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin aestīvāticum, from Latin aestīvus (“relating to summer”).
Inherited from Old French estencele, from Vulgar Latin *stincilla, a metathesis of Latin scintilla.

parole.significato: to caulk (block using oakum or by extension another similar material)
parole.testo: Recorded in Old French as estoper, estuper. From Vulgar Latin *stuppāre, from Latin stuppa. Equivalent to étoupe + -er. Compare Occitan estopar, Italian stoppare, Old Spanish estopar; cf. also Romanian astupa, Romansh stuppar, Venetan stupar, Sicilian stuppari.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exturdīre, from turdus (“thrush”). Compare Italian stordire.
From Old French estriller, from Vulgar Latin *strigiliāre, from *strigila, from Latin strigilis.
From Old French estrecier, from Vulgar Latin *strictiāre, from Latin strictus (“narrow”).

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: case (for glasses, cigars, soap, a viola)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French étui, from Old French estui (“case, sheath”), of uncertain origin. Possibly a derivative of Old French estuier (“keep, hold”), itself possibly from Vulgar Latin *studiāre, from Latin studium; or, more likely, of Germanic origin, related to Middle High German stūche (“cup
Inherited from Old French esvanir, evanir, probably from a Vulgar Latin *exvānīre, later influenced from the Latin form ēvānuit (“vanished”) of ēvānescō, ēvānēscere.
Inherited from Middle French esveiller, from Old French esveiller, esveillier, from Vulgar Latin *exviglāre < *exvigilāre, from Latin ēvigilāre.

parole.significato: to air, ventilate (expose to the air)
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exventāre, from Latin ventus (“wind”). By surface analysis, é- + vent + -er. Compare Occitan esventar.
Originally written isle; from Middle French isle, from Old French isle, from Vulgar Latin *īsula, from Classical Latin īnsula.

parole.significato: eye, organ that is sensitive to light, helping organisms to see
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle French œil, from Old French oil, uel, ueil (plural olz, ialz), from Vulgar Latin oclus, from Latin oculus. Doublet of oculus, a borrowing. Cognate with Spanish ojo, Portuguese olho, Galician ollo, Italian occhio, Romanian ochi and Catalan ull. For the phonetic development of th
Inherited from Middle French œuf, from Old French oef, from Vulgar Latin (*)ŏvum, from Classical Latin ōvum. Compare Occitan uòu.
From fil, or from Vulgar Latin *affilāre, from Latin fīlum. Compare Italian affilare, Spanish afilar, Portuguese afiar.

Inherited from Old French afronter (“to face; to confront; to slap in the face”), either a French derivation a- + front + -er, or an inheritance from an unattested Vulgar Latin *affrontāre (“to strike against”), from Latin ad + frontem. Compare Italian affrontare.

Inherited from Middle French ailleurs, from Old French aillors, aillurs (“elsewhere”), probably from Latin aliōrsum, or from a Vulgar Latin *aliore, from in *aliore loco. Possibly connected to Latin aliubī, from alibī. Compare with Occitan alhors, Portuguese alhures and Romanian aiurea.
Most likely from a- + long + -er, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *allongāre, from ad + Late Latin longāre, from Latin longus.
Inherited from Old French anee. By surface analysis, an + -ée; an (“year”) from Latin annus (“year”). Perhaps alternatively from a Vulgar Latin *annāta, from Latin annāre; compare Italian annata.

Inherited from Old French baston, probably from a Vulgar Latin bastōnem, itself a modification of Late Latin bastum, or possibly noun use of the verb *bastāre, from Ancient Greek βαστάζω (bastázō). Compare Italian bastone.

parole.significato: to nail in, put a nail in
parole.testo: From Old French encloer. By surface analysis, en- + clou + -er. Or alternatively from Vulgar Latin *inclāvāre, from Late Latin clāvāre, from Latin clāvus.

parole.significato: Spanish, from or otherwise related to Spain, its people etc.
parole.testo: From Spanish español or from Middle French espaignol, from Old French espagneul or espaigneul, borrowed from Old Occitan espaignol, espainol, from a Vulgar Latin *Hispaniolus, from Latin Hispānus, from Hispania. Doublet of épagneul and Pagnol.
From espérer + -ance (Middle French and Old French esperance), or possibly corresponding to Vulgar Latin spērantia, from Latin spērāns. Compare Italian speranza, Spanish esperanza, Catalan esperança.

parole.significato: synonym of thym (aromatic herb used in cooking)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Occitan ferigoulo, farigoulo, from Old Occitan farigola, from Vulgar Latin *fericula < ferus. OR from Medieval Latin *ferricula < fer, influenced by auricula, lenticula, sanicula as well as ferraria.
